name: AI Agents and MCP in Depth
level: In-depth engineering course · no official exam

lessons.title: Workflows vs agents: the five patterns
lessons.summary: Tell a workflow from an agent, match each of the five composable patterns to the problem it fits, and know when a plain workflow is the better build.

sections.heading: Two kinds of agentic system
sections.body:
Anthropic's *Building effective agents* draws one line through the whole space:

- **Workflows** are "systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths". Your code decides the order of steps.
- **Agents** are systems where LLMs "dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage". The model decides the next step.

Both are useful. The difference is **who holds control flow**. A workflow is predictable, cheap to test and easy to debug. An agent is flexible but costs more tokens and latency, and its errors can compound over many steps.

The guiding rule is to find "the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed". Often that is a single well-prompted call with retrieval, not an agent at all.

sections.heading: The five workflow patterns
sections.body:
| Pattern | What it does | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| Prompt chaining | Each call processes the previous call's output; code can check results between steps | "the task can be easily and cleanly decomposed into fixed subtasks" |
| Routing | A classifier step sends the input to a specialised prompt, tool set or model | there are "distinct categories that are better handled separately" |
| Parallelisation | **Sectioning** splits work into independent parts; **voting** runs the same task several times | "the divided subtasks can be parallelized for speed", or several attempts give more confidence |
| Orchestrator-workers | A central LLM breaks the task down at run time and delegates to workers | "complex tasks where you can't predict the subtasks needed" |
| Evaluator-optimiser | One call generates, another evaluates and gives feedback in a loop | "when we have clear evaluation criteria" |

The key contrast is **orchestrator-workers vs parallelisation**. In sectioning, *you* fix the subtasks in code. In orchestrator-workers, the *model* decides the subtasks for each input.

sections.heading: When an agent is warranted
sections.body:
Agents fit "open-ended problems where it's difficult or impossible to predict the required number of steps", where you cannot hard-code a path. Signs you are there:

- The number and kind of steps vary a lot between inputs.
- The model needs feedback from the environment (tool results, test runs) to choose the next step.
- A simpler pattern has been tried and measured, and it falls short.

Signs a plain workflow wins: the steps are known, the task must be auditable step by step, latency and cost budgets are tight, or a wrong action is expensive.

sections.heading: Three principles for any design
sections.body:
1. **Simplicity.** Keep the design as small as the task allows.
2. **Transparency.** Show the agent's planning steps explicitly so people can see and debug them.
3. **A well-crafted agent-computer interface (ACI).** Invest in tool documentation and testing as much as in prompts.

The post's poka-yoke example: a coding agent kept making mistakes with relative file paths, so the team changed the tool to **require absolute paths**, and the error class disappeared. Changing the tool beat adding more prompt instructions.

Note: the post now carries an update saying "Much of the tooling landscape described in this post has changed since December 2024". The patterns still hold. The framework names it mentions may not.

keyPoints: Workflows run on predefined code paths; agents let the model direct its own process and tool use.
Start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when measurement shows you need it.
Prompt chaining: fixed subtasks. Routing: distinct input categories. Parallelisation: independent parts or voting.
Orchestrator-workers: subtasks you cannot predict up front. Evaluator-optimiser: clear evaluation criteria.
Agents fit open-ended problems where the number of steps cannot be predicted.
Fix recurring agent mistakes in the tool interface (poka-yoke), not only in the prompt.

gotchas.trap: Orchestrator-workers and sectioning are the same thing.
gotchas.correct: In sectioning, code fixes the subtasks. In orchestrator-workers, the model chooses the subtasks for each input.

gotchas.trap: An agent is always the more capable design, so build one by default.
gotchas.correct: An agent trades cost, latency and predictability for flexibility. Use one only when a fixed path cannot do the job.

gotchas.trap: Evaluator-optimiser works for any task.
gotchas.correct: It only pays off when there are clear evaluation criteria and feedback measurably improves the output.

lessons.lab: Take one task from your own work (for example, support triage or a report generator). Sketch it three ways: one call, the best-fitting workflow pattern, and a full agent. For each, list the number of model calls, the points where code can check results, and what a failure looks like. Pick the simplest one that meets the bar and write one sentence on why.

lessons.title: The agent loop, stop conditions and budgets
lessons.summary: Build the core loop correctly: call the model, run requested tools, feed back observations, and stop on the right signal or when a budget runs out.

sections.heading: The core loop
sections.body:
Every tool-using agent runs the same loop:

1. Send the conversation and tool definitions to the model.
2. If the response asks for tools, run them in your code.
3. Append the results as **observations** (`tool_result` blocks on Claude) and call the model again.
4. Stop when the model finishes or a policy limit is hit.

On Claude, the loop continues while `stop_reason == "tool_use"`. Tool results must come straight after the assistant turn that called them, and all results for parallel calls go in a single user message.

```python
for step in range(MAX_STEPS):
    resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, tools=TOOLS, messages=msgs, max_tokens=4096)
    msgs.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    results = [run_tool(b) for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    msgs.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
```

sections.heading: Reading stop reasons
sections.body:
Branch on `stop_reason`, not on whether the response contains text. A response can hold text *and* `tool_use` blocks.

- `tool_use`: run the tools and continue.
- `end_turn`: the model considers the turn finished.
- `max_tokens`: output was cut off. Treat it as **incomplete**. Do not run a truncated tool call; raise the limit or handle the partial output.
- `stop_sequence`: one of your stop sequences was hit.
- Other values (for example a refusal, a server-tool pause, or the context window running out) each need their own handling. Check the stop-reasons page for the current list rather than assuming it is fixed.

sections.heading: Errors are observations too
sections.body:
When a tool fails, do not crash the loop and do not hide the failure. Return a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` and an instructive message, such as "Rate limit exceeded. Retry after 60 seconds." The model can then retry, change approach, or tell the user.

With invalid or missing parameters, Claude tends to retry a few times with corrections before giving up, so a clear error message saves steps.

sections.heading: Iteration and token budgets

keyPoints: Loop while stop_reason is tool_use; branch on stop_reason, not on the presence of text.
Tool results go immediately after the calling assistant turn, all parallel results in one user message.
max_tokens means truncated output, not success.
Return tool failures as is_error results with actionable messages so the model can recover.
Iteration caps, token budgets and timeouts are client-side policy you must enforce.
Per-step reliability compounds: 0.95 per step over 20 steps is only about 36% end to end.

gotchas.trap: The loop can stop as soon as the response contains text.
gotchas.correct: Claude can return text and tool_use blocks together. Use stop_reason.

gotchas.trap: The model will always stop by itself, so no cap is needed.
gotchas.correct: Enforce a maximum step count, a token budget and timeouts in your code.

gotchas.trap: Throwing an exception on a tool failure is the safe option.
gotchas.correct: Return the failure as a tool_result with is_error: true so the model sees it and can adapt.

lessons.lab: Write a minimal loop against one harmless tool (for example a calculator). Add a step cap of 5, a cumulative token budget from the usage fields, and a fake tool that fails every other call with is_error: true. Log stop_reason on every turn and confirm the loop stops for the right reason in each case.

lessons.title: Planning and reasoning patterns
lessons.summary: Compare ReAct, plan-and-execute and reflection, and steer reasoning on current Claude models with adaptive thinking and effort rather than legacy thinking budgets.

sections.heading: ReAct: reason, act, observe
sections.body:
ReAct (Yao et al., ICLR 2023) **interleaves reasoning traces with actions**. The model thinks about what it needs, calls a tool such as search, reads the observation, and reasons again.

- Reasoning helps the model plan and handle exceptions.
- Actions ground the reasoning in outside information, which reduces made-up facts.
- On ALFWorld and WebShop it beat imitation and reinforcement-learning baselines by 34 and 10 points of absolute success, with only one or two in-context examples.

A modern tool-use loop is essentially ReAct: each turn the model decides the next action from the latest observation.

sections.heading: Plan-and-execute
sections.body:
Plan-and-execute splits the work in two:

1. A planning step writes an explicit list of steps.
2. An executor runs the steps, and the system **replans** when a step fails or the facts change.

Trade-offs against step-by-step ReAct:

| | ReAct | Plan-and-execute |
|---|---|---|
| Adapts to surprises | Every step | At replanning points |
| Plan is visible up front | No | Yes, so a human can review it |
| Model calls | One decision per step | Fewer planner calls; executors can be cheaper |

An explicit plan also serves the *transparency* principle from *Building effective agents*: show the planning steps.

sections.heading: Reflection and Reflexion
sections.body:
Reflection means the agent critiques its own attempt and tries again. **Reflexion** (Shinn et al., 2023) makes this concrete:

- After a failure, the agent writes a **verbal self-reflection**.
- The reflection is stored in an **episodic memory buffer** and added to the next attempt.
- No model weights change.

It reported 91% pass@1 on HumanEval against 80% for GPT-4. Reflection works best with a real feedback signal (tests, a checker, an evaluator), which is the same reason evaluator-optimiser needs clear criteria.

sections.heading: Thinking on current Claude models
sections.body:
Current Claude models use **adaptive thinking**: the model decides how much to think, and you steer it with the **`effort`** parameter. Default effort differs by model (for example `medium` on Opus 5.5 and `high` on Sonnet 5.5), and on some models adaptive thinking is always on.

The older control, `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}`, is deprecated on Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 and **not accepted on later models**. Code that sets a fixed thinking budget is legacy.

Practical guidance:

- Raise effort for hard planning or multi-step reasoning steps.
- Lower effort for simple, latency-sensitive steps such as routing or classification.
- Changing thinking or effort settings between requests invalidates cached messages, so keep them stable within a conversation.

keyPoints: ReAct interleaves reasoning with tool actions so each step is grounded in a fresh observation.
Plan-and-execute writes the plan first, then executes and replans; the plan can be reviewed.
Reflexion stores verbal self-reflections in episodic memory; no weight updates.
Reflection needs a real feedback signal such as tests or an evaluator.
On current Claude models, steer reasoning with effort; manual budget_tokens is not accepted after the 4.6 generation.

gotchas.trap: Set thinking.budget_tokens to control reasoning on the newest Claude models.
gotchas.correct: That control is not accepted on post-4.6 models. Use adaptive thinking with the effort parameter.

gotchas.trap: Reflexion fine-tunes the model on its failures.
gotchas.correct: Reflexion keeps the weights fixed and stores reflections as text in memory.

gotchas.trap: A plan written up front removes the need to adapt.
gotchas.correct: Plan-and-execute must replan when a step fails or new facts appear.

lessons.lab: Take one multi-step research question. Run it once as a free ReAct loop and once as plan-then-execute where you print the plan before any tool call. Compare the number of tool calls, total tokens and whether the plan would have let a reviewer catch a bad step early.

lessons.title: Multi-agent systems and context isolation
lessons.summary: Decide when sub-agents earn their extra tokens, use them for context isolation, pass state between agents safely, and know when one agent is better.

sections.heading: What sub-agents buy you
sections.body:
A sub-agent is a separate model loop with its own fresh context window. The lead agent gives it a task; it explores and returns a **condensed summary**, "often around 1,000–2,000 tokens", instead of all the raw material it read.

Benefits:

- **Context isolation.** The lead's window stays small and on topic.
- **Parallel breadth.** Independent lines of inquiry run at the same time.
- **Separation of concerns.** Each worker gets its own tools and instructions.

In Anthropic's research system, an Opus 4 lead with Sonnet 4 sub-agents beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on an internal research eval.

sections.heading: What it costs
sections.body:
Agents use about **4x** the tokens of chat, and multi-agent systems about **15x**. In that analysis, token usage alone explained about 80% of the variance in performance on BrowseComp. More agents is largely a way to spend more tokens in parallel.

So multi-agent designs pay off only on **high-value tasks** where breadth-first, parallel exploration helps. Scale effort to the task: simple fact-finding needs one agent with a handful of tool calls; complex research may justify many sub-agents.

sections.heading: When one agent is better
sections.body:
Multi-agent systems are a poor fit for tasks that need **shared context** or have **many dependencies between agents**. The post names "most coding work" as an example: a refactor where every file depends on decisions made in others is better done by one agent holding the whole picture.

Other warning signs: sub-tasks that must agree on a shared design, a tight cost budget, or work that is inherently sequential.

sections.heading: Hand-offs and shared state
sections.body:
Every hand-off between agents is a lossy summary. Design for it:

- Give each sub-agent a **clear task description**: objective, output format, tools to use, and boundaries.
- Ask for a **structured, condensed** result, not a transcript.
- Keep durable state **outside the context window** (structured notes, files or a store referenced by identifier) so agents pass references rather than retelling content.
- Remember that synchronous batches, where the lead waits for every sub-agent, are a throughput bottleneck.

sections.heading: Reliability for long multi-agent runs

keyPoints: Sub-agents give context isolation: they explore in clean windows and return 1,000 to 2,000 token summaries.
Multi-agent systems use about 15x the tokens of chat; reserve them for high-value, parallelisable tasks.
Tasks with shared context or tight dependencies, such as most coding work, usually suit one agent.
Pass state by reference to durable notes or stores, not by retelling it in chat.
Resume long runs from checkpoints and combine retries with agent adaptation.

gotchas.trap: More sub-agents always means better results.
gotchas.correct: Gains come largely from spending more tokens; on dependent or shared-context tasks a single agent is often better and far cheaper.

gotchas.trap: Sub-agents should return everything they found so the lead misses nothing.
gotchas.correct: Return condensed summaries; raw dumps defeat context isolation.

gotchas.trap: A failed step means restarting the whole multi-agent run.
gotchas.correct: Checkpoint state and resume from the last good point.

lessons.lab: Pick a research question with three independent sub-topics. Run it with one agent, then with a lead plus three sub-agents that each return a summary under 1,500 tokens. Record total tokens, wall-clock time and answer quality against a short rubric, and decide whether the multi-agent version earned its cost.

lessons.title: Human-in-the-loop and durable execution
lessons.summary: Put humans at the right gates, pause and resume runs without server-side sessions, and keep long-running work durable across failures.

sections.heading: Approval gates
Interrupts and pause-resume in MCP
sections.body:
MCP revision 2026-07-28 is stateless and **servers no longer send requests to clients**. When a server needs input in the middle of `tools/call`, `resources/read` or `prompts/get`, it uses **Multi Round-Trip Requests (MRTR)**:

1. The server returns a result with `resultType: "input_required"` (an `InputRequiredResult`) listing the input it needs, for example an `elicitation/create` request.
2. The client gathers the answer, often from the user.
3. The client **retries the original request with a new JSON-RPC id**, attaching `inputResponses` and echoing `requestState` exactly.

Rules for `requestState`: the client must not inspect or change it. The server must treat it as attacker-controlled, integrity-protect it (HMAC or AEAD) when it affects authorisation or business logic, and should bind it to the principal, a short TTL and the originating request. Those bindings limit replay but do not make it single-use, so a server whose state must be consumed at most once has to enforce that itself. A server must not ask for input types the client has not declared.

sections.heading: Asking the user safely
sections.body:
Elicitation **form mode** is for simple, flat data (strings, numbers, booleans, enums). It **must not** request passwords, API keys, tokens or payment credentials; those go through **URL mode**, where the client shows the full URL and opens it in a context the client and model cannot inspect. In URL mode, `accept` means the user consented to open the link, not that the flow finished.

The user's responses are `accept`, `decline` or `cancel`, and the agent must handle all three.

sections.heading: Durable, resumable runs
sections.body:
Long runs fail: processes restart, networks drop, users go home. Durable execution means the run can continue from where it stopped.

- **Checkpoint** state after each meaningful step (messages, tool results, plan position) to storage you control, and resume from the last checkpoint.
- Make side-effecting steps safe to repeat, so a resumed run does not, for example, charge a card twice.
- For long server-side jobs, MCP offers the **Tasks extension** (`io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks`): a durable handle the client polls with `tasks/get` and can send input to with `tasks/update`.
- Do not rely on keeping one HTTP stream open. In 2026-07-28, SSE resumability (`Last-Event-ID`) is removed; a broken stream loses the request and the client must re-issue it with a new id.

keyPoints: A human should be able to deny tool invocations; confirm sensitive operations and show inputs first.
Tool annotations are hints from the server and are untrusted unless the server is trusted.
MRTR: the server returns input_required, the client retries with a new id, inputResponses and the exact requestState.
Servers integrity-protect requestState and bind it to the principal, a short TTL and the originating request; single use needs separate server-side enforcement.
Never collect secrets through form-mode elicitation; use URL mode.
Checkpoint long runs and use a durable task handle rather than one long-lived stream.

gotchas.trap: The server can push an elicitation request to the client at any time over a GET stream.
gotchas.correct: In 2026-07-28 the GET stream and server-initiated requests are gone; use MRTR.

gotchas.trap: Reuse the same JSON-RPC id when retrying after input_required.
gotchas.correct: The retry must use a new id and echo requestState unchanged.

gotchas.trap: destructiveHint: false from any server means no approval is needed.
gotchas.correct: Annotations are untrusted unless the server is trusted; keep your own approval policy.

lessons.lab: Add an approval gate to an agent loop: classify each tool as read or write, auto-run reads, and pause on writes by saving the conversation to disk and printing the proposed call. Kill the process, restart it, load the checkpoint, approve the call and confirm the run completes without repeating earlier steps.

lessons.title: Writing tools agents can use
lessons.summary: A tool is a contract with a non-deterministic caller. Good names, detailed descriptions, precise schemas and a deliberately small surface matter more than wrapping every endpoint you have.

sections.heading: Tools are not API wrappers
sections.body:
Anthropic's guidance is blunt: do not wrap every endpoint. An agent has limited context, and every call it makes costs tokens and a chance to go wrong.

- Prefer **`search_contacts`** over **`list_contacts`**. Listing everything forces the agent to read thousands of rows to find one; a search tool does the filtering where it is cheap.
- **Consolidate multi-step work** into one tool when the steps always happen together. A `schedule_event` tool that finds availability and books the slot beats three tools the agent must chain correctly every time.
- Build tools around **the tasks agents actually do**, then check with evaluations that they help.

The Claude docs say the same thing from the other side: "consolidate related operations into fewer tools", for example one tool with an `action` parameter rather than separate `create_pr`, `review_pr` and `merge_pr` tools.

sections.heading: Names and namespaces
sections.body:
Names are the first thing the model reads when picking a tool.

- **Namespace by service and resource**: `asana_search`, `asana_projects_search`. When several servers are connected, prefixes stop two `search` tools from colliding. Prefix and suffix naming can change results, so evaluate both.
- **Claude's name rule** is `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$`. No dots.
- **MCP tool names may also contain `.`**, so an MCP tool called `admin.tools.list` must be renamed (say `admin_tools_list`) before it can be sent as a Claude tool.
- MCP clients that aggregate servers SHOULD disambiguate names, for example with a server prefix, and should not rely on `serverInfo.name` being unique.

sections.heading: Descriptions and schemas
Tool bloat and tool search
Evaluate, do not guess
sections.body: Tool design is evaluation-driven. Build realistic, multi-step tasks, keep a held-out set, and track more than accuracy: runtime, number of tool calls, tokens consumed and tool errors. Read the transcripts. When the agent calls the wrong tool or passes a bad argument, the fix is usually in the name, description or schema, not in the system prompt.

keyPoints: Build tools around tasks: search beats list, and one tool that does a common multi-step job beats a chain of thin wrappers.
Namespace tool names by service and resource; Claude names must match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$, so dotted MCP names need renaming.
Descriptions should be three to four sentences or more: what, when, parameters, limitations.
Selection quality drops past roughly 30 to 50 tools; use tool search with deferred loading instead of loading everything.
Judge tool changes with evaluations that track accuracy, calls, tokens and errors.

gotchas.trap: Expose one tool per REST endpoint so the agent has full flexibility.
gotchas.correct: Expose fewer, task-shaped tools (search, consolidated actions). Thin wrappers waste context and multiply wrong choices.

gotchas.trap: Keep tool descriptions to one line to save tokens.
gotchas.correct: Detailed descriptions are the main lever on tool selection; the docs ask for at least three to four sentences.

gotchas.trap: Defer every tool behind tool search to minimise tokens.
gotchas.correct: At least one tool must stay non-deferred, or the request returns 400.

lessons.lab: Take an MCP server you use and list its tools. Rewrite the three most-used ones: namespace the names, expand each description to cover what, when, parameters and limits, and rename any vague parameter. Run ten realistic tasks before and after and compare tool-call count, tokens and wrong-tool errors.

sources.title: Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering

lessons.title: Tool-call mechanics on Claude and OpenAI
lessons.summary: The round trip is simple but strict: where results go, how parallel calls are answered, how tool_choice and strict schemas behave, and which tools you must never execute yourself.

sections.heading: The Claude round trip
sections.body:
When Claude wants a tool, the response has `stop_reason: "tool_use"` and one or more `tool_use` blocks, each with an `id`, `name` and `input`. Your code runs them and replies with a `user` message of `tool_result` blocks.

Placement rules that cause most 400s:

- Tool results must **immediately follow** the assistant turn that requested them.
- In that user message, **`tool_result` blocks come first**. Text may follow them; text before them is a 400.
- **All results for a parallel batch go in one user message**, one `tool_result` per `tool_use_id`.

~~~json
{ "role": "user", "content": [
  { "type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_01A", "content": "72°F, clear" },
  { "type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_01B", "content": "55°F, rain" },
  { "type": "text", "text": "Compare the two." }
]}
~~~

sections.heading: Parallel calls
sections.body:
Claude may request several independent tools in one turn. That is usually good (less latency, fewer turns). When calls must run in order, for example because the second depends on a side effect of the first, turn it off:

~~~json
"tool_choice": { "type": "auto", "disable_parallel_tool_use": true }
~~~

On OpenAI the switch is `parallel_tool_calls: false`, which means at most one call per turn.

sections.heading: tool_choice and forced calls
sections.body:
Claude's `tool_choice` values:

- `auto`: the model decides. It is the default when tools are present (`none` is the default when they are absent).
- `any`: must call some tool. `tool`: must call the named tool.
- `none`: no tool calls.

Two cautions. Changing `tool_choice` invalidates cached messages. And forced calls are not universal any more: on several current Claude models (at the time of writing, including Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5) `any` and `tool` return a 400, and where forcing is still accepted a forced call skips thinking. The documented replacement is `auto` with `strict: true` on the tool, or structured outputs when you only need a JSON answer. Check the define-tools page for the current model list before relying on forcing.

OpenAI's `tool_choice` offers `auto`, `required`, a forced `{type:"function", name}`, `none`, and `allowed_tools`, which restricts the usable set while preserving the prompt cache.

sections.heading: Strict schemas
OpenAI Responses round trip
sections.body:
OpenAI tools are `{type: "function", name, description, parameters, strict}`. The model emits `function_call` items with a `call_id`, `name` and `arguments` as a **JSON string** you must parse. You answer with a `function_call_output` item carrying the same `call_id` and an `output` string. With reasoning models, pass the reasoning items back along with the tool outputs.

OpenAI also has custom tools that take free text, optionally constrained by a Lark or regex grammar.

sections.heading: Client tools versus server tools
sections.body:
On Claude, **client tools** run in your application: your own functions plus Anthropic-schema tools such as `bash`, `text_editor`, memory, computer and browser toolsets. **Server tools** (web search, web fetch, code execution, tool search, the MCP connector) run on Anthropic's infrastructure and Anthropic supplies their results. Usually they arrive in the same response; when Claude calls a server tool in the same parallel batch as client tools, the server result can arrive in a later response.

Never send a `tool_result` for a server tool call (ids starting `srvtoolu_`). Your loop should execute, and answer, only client `tool_use` blocks. If the assistant turn also contains a server tool call that has no result yet, the user message must contain only `tool_result` blocks, with no trailing text.

Finally, keep untrusted content (web pages, emails, files) inside `tool_result` blocks, not in the system prompt or plain user text.

keyPoints: tool_result blocks immediately follow the requesting turn, come first in the user content, and all parallel results share one user message.
Disable parallel calls with disable_parallel_tool_use (Claude) or parallel_tool_calls: false (OpenAI) when order matters.
Forced tool_choice returns 400 on several current Claude models; use auto plus strict: true or structured outputs instead.
OpenAI strict mode needs additionalProperties: false, every field required, and nullable types for optional fields.
OpenAI arguments arrive as a JSON string; answer with function_call_output and the same call_id.
Never return a tool_result for a server tool (srvtoolu_) id.

gotchas.trap: Put a short text note before the tool_result blocks to explain them.
gotchas.correct: tool_result blocks must come first in the user content; text goes after them or the request returns 400.

gotchas.trap: Send each parallel tool result in its own user message.
gotchas.correct: All results for one assistant turn go in a single user message.

gotchas.trap: Use tool_choice any to guarantee a call on every model.
gotchas.correct: Forced choice returns 400 on several current models and skips thinking where it is allowed; prefer auto with strict schemas.

lessons.lab: Write a minimal agent loop against the Messages API with two tools. Ask a question that triggers parallel calls and confirm both results go in one user message. Then deliberately put a text block before the tool_result and observe the 400. Finally turn on disable_parallel_tool_use and compare the transcript.

lessons.title: Tool outputs and errors that help the model
lessons.summary: Whatever a tool returns lands in the context window. Return what the agent needs, in as few tokens as possible, with identifiers it can reuse and errors it can act on.

sections.heading: Return meaning, not internals
sections.body:
Agents reason better over names than opaque codes. Anthropic found that resolving UUIDs to human-readable names "reduced hallucinations". Return the fields the next decision needs, and leave out internal metadata.

Offer a **`response_format`** enum. In Anthropic's example a `detailed` response was 206 tokens and a `concise` one 72. The detailed form keeps the identifiers the agent needs for follow-up calls; the concise form is for when it only needs to read.

sections.heading: Token efficiency: paginate, filter, truncate
Errors are results
sections.body:
A tool failure is information the model can use, so return it as a result rather than crashing the loop.

- **Claude**: return a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` and an instructive message, such as "Rate limit exceeded. Retry after 60 seconds."
- **MCP** separates two kinds of error. **Protocol errors** (unknown tool, malformed request) are JSON-RPC errors such as `-32602`. **Tool execution errors** (an upstream API failed, input failed validation, a business rule refused) go in the result with `isError: true`, so the model can self-correct. Clients SHOULD pass execution errors to the model.

An actionable error names the problem and the next step: "No order ord_missing. Use search_orders to find IDs." beats "404".

sections.heading: Structured output and stable identifiers

keyPoints: Resolve opaque ids to names and return only decision-relevant fields; offer a concise/detailed response_format.
Paginate, filter, range-select and, as a last resort, truncate with guidance on how to get more.
Return failures as results: is_error: true on Claude, isError: true for MCP tool execution errors.
MCP protocol errors (unknown tool, malformed request) are JSON-RPC errors; execution errors are results the model sees.
structuredContent must match outputSchema, with the JSON also serialized in a text block for compatibility.
State handles are opaque, high-entropy, re-authorized on every call and documented with a lifetime.

gotchas.trap: Raise an exception from the tool so the agent loop stops cleanly on failure.
gotchas.correct: Return the error as a tool result with guidance; the model can often retry or take another path.

gotchas.trap: Report input-validation failures as JSON-RPC protocol errors.
gotchas.correct: In MCP, validation and business-logic failures are tool execution errors (isError: true) so the model can self-correct.

gotchas.trap: Treat a session or state handle as proof of who the caller is.
gotchas.correct: Check authorization on every call and bind handles to the verified user id.

lessons.lab: Pick a tool that returns a large list. Add a response_format enum, a cursor-based page parameter and a filter. Measure tokens per call before and after on five tasks, and rewrite every error string so it names the next action.

lessons.title: Side-effecting tools: idempotency, dry runs, confirmation
lessons.summary: Agents retry, repeat and misjudge. Tools that change the world need to be safe to call twice, previewable before they act, gated by a human when the stakes are high, and reversible where possible.

sections.heading: Why agents need idempotent writes
Dry runs and previews
sections.body: Give destructive or bulk tools a `dry_run` (or `preview`) mode that returns exactly what would change ("would delete 312 files under /tmp/export, total 4.1 GB") without changing anything. The agent, or a human, can then confirm with a second call that carries the same parameters, or a plan id returned by the preview so the confirmed action cannot drift from what was shown.

sections.heading: Confirmation and the human in the loop
Rollback and compensation

keyPoints: Generate one idempotency key per logical operation and reuse it on retries; the server returns the stored result for repeats.
Give bulk and destructive tools a dry-run that returns the exact change set before anything happens.
MCP clients SHOULD confirm sensitive operations and show inputs before calling.
Annotation defaults: readOnlyHint false, destructiveHint true, idempotentHint false, openWorldHint true.
Annotations from untrusted servers are hints, not guarantees; never auto-approve on them alone.
Prefer reversible operations and keep an audit trail that supports compensating actions.

gotchas.trap: Generate a new idempotency key inside the HTTP client on every attempt.
gotchas.correct: The key identifies the logical operation; reuse it across retries or it protects nothing.

gotchas.trap: Auto-approve any tool whose annotations say readOnlyHint: true.
gotchas.correct: Annotations are untrusted unless the server is trusted; a malicious server can mislabel destructive tools.

gotchas.trap: A tool with no annotations is safe because it declares no destructive behaviour.
gotchas.correct: The defaults assume a non-read-only, destructive, non-idempotent, open-world tool.

lessons.lab: Wrap a write tool (create issue, send message) with an idempotency key supplied by your loop. Simulate a timeout after the server acted and confirm the retry returns the original result. Then add a dry_run flag and a confirmation step to a bulk-delete tool.

lessons.title: Code execution and computer use as tools
lessons.summary: Letting an agent run code or drive a computer is powerful and dangerous. The power comes from doing work outside the context window; the safety comes from sandboxes with both filesystem and network isolation, timeouts and resource limits.

sections.heading: Code as the tool interface
Sandboxes need both walls
sections.body:
Anthropic's Claude Code sandboxing write-up states that "effective sandboxing requires *both* filesystem and network isolation":

- **filesystem isolation alone** still lets compromised code send whatever it can read (source, tokens) to an attacker;
- **network isolation alone** still lets it read or modify sensitive files such as SSH keys or shell profiles.

Claude Code builds this on OS primitives (Linux bubblewrap, macOS seatbelt) and routes network traffic through a proxy that only allows approved domains. A side benefit: with safe defaults the agent needs fewer approvals; Anthropic reports sandboxing reduced permission prompts by 84%.

sections.heading: Timeouts and resource limits
Computer use and browser toolsets
sections.body:
Computer use lets the model operate a desktop from screenshots, mouse and keyboard; browser toolsets do the same for a browser. They are Anthropic-schema **client tools**: your code executes the actions, so isolation is your responsibility. Run them in a dedicated VM or container with minimal privileges, keep untrusted page content in tool results, and require a human for consequential actions such as purchases or sending messages.

These tool types are **versioned** and old versions are retired. At the time of writing the release notes say computer use requires `computer_toolset_20260801` and the older `computer_20251124` returns 400 outside Bedrock. Check the release notes rather than copying a version string from an old example.

keyPoints: Presenting MCP servers as code APIs lets the agent filter data in a sandbox; Anthropic's example went from 150,000 to 2,000 tokens.
Effective sandboxing needs both filesystem and network isolation.
Claude Code's sandbox uses bubblewrap (Linux) and seatbelt (macOS) with a domain-restricting network proxy.
Every execution needs a timeout, CPU/memory/disk limits, restricted egress and no ambient credentials.
Computer use and browser toolsets are client tools: you run them, so you isolate them; their versions change, so check the release notes.

gotchas.trap: Mounting only the project directory is enough sandboxing.
gotchas.correct: Without network isolation, code can still exfiltrate whatever it can read.

gotchas.trap: Code execution saves tokens, so it is a pure win.
gotchas.correct: It shifts risk into the execution environment, which needs sandboxing, resource limits and monitoring.

lessons.lab: Run an agent's code-execution step inside a container with no network, a 30-second timeout and a 512 MB memory cap. Then allow a single domain through a proxy and confirm that a request to any other host fails.

lessons.title: MCP architecture: roles, primitives, capabilities and versions
lessons.summary: How the Model Context Protocol splits work between hosts, clients and servers, which primitives a server exposes and who controls each one, and how the 2026-07-28 revision negotiates capabilities and protocol versions on every request instead of in a handshake.

sections.heading: Hosts, clients and servers
sections.body:
MCP is JSON-RPC 2.0 between three roles:

- A **host** is the LLM application the user runs (a chat app, an IDE, an agent runtime).
- A **client** is a connector inside the host. Each client talks to one server.
- A **server** exposes context and capabilities to the host through that client.

The host owns the model, the user interface and the consent decisions. A server never sees the whole conversation; it sees only the requests its client sends. Keeping that split in mind answers most design questions: anything that needs the user's judgment belongs in the host, and anything that needs the backing system's data belongs in the server.

The 2026-07-28 base protocol is described as **stateless, self-contained requests** with **per-request capability negotiation**.

sections.heading: The three server primitives and who controls them
sections.body:
A server can offer three kinds of feature, and the spec assigns each a controller:

| Primitive | Control | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **Prompts** | User-controlled | slash commands, menu options |
| **Resources** | Application-controlled | file contents, git history |
| **Tools** | Model-controlled | API POST requests, writing files |

Resources are context and data for the user or the model to use; the host application decides what to attach. Prompts are templated messages and workflows the user picks. Tools are functions the model decides to call. Choosing the wrong primitive is a classic design error: a read-only report the user always wants attached is a resource or a prompt, not a tool the model has to remember to call.

sections.heading: Client features, utilities and extensions
sections.body:
In 2026-07-28 the only non-deprecated client feature is **elicitation**: the server asks the user, through the host, for input. **Sampling** and **Roots** are deprecated, as is protocol-level **Logging**.

Utilities shared by both sides cover configuration, progress, cancellation and error reporting.

Optional **extensions** are negotiated in `capabilities.extensions`. Examples in this revision are **Tasks** (moved out of the core into an extension), **Skills over MCP** and **MCP Apps** (`io.modelcontextprotocol/ui`). A client that has not declared an extension must not be sent its features.

sections.heading: Capabilities travel on every request
sections.body:
There is no session in which capabilities are agreed once. Every request carries `_meta` with:

- `io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion` (required)
- `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities` (required)
- `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo` (should)
- `io.modelcontextprotocol/logLevel` (optional)

A request missing a required field is rejected with `-32602` (HTTP 400). Results should carry `io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo`. Client and server info are **self-reported**, so they should not drive security decisions.

Every result also carries `resultType`, either `"complete"` or `"input_required"`. A result from an older server with no `resultType` is treated as complete.

sections.heading: Versioning without a handshake
sections.body:
The `initialize` handshake is gone. The client simply sends its version on each request. If the server does not support it, it answers `-32022` (UnsupportedProtocolVersion) with `data: { supported: [...], requested }`, and the client retries with a version from that list.

Servers **must** implement `server/discover`; clients may call it first to learn versions and capabilities. To detect a legacy server, a client probes with `server/discover` on stdio, or on HTTP attempts a modern request and falls back to `initialize` only if a 400 body is not a recognised modern error. A server may serve both eras on one endpoint.

Deprecated features stay for a minimum **12-month** window before removal, so a deprecation is a signal to plan migration, not an outage.

keyPoints: Host = the LLM app; client = one connector inside it; server = the exposed capability. JSON-RPC 2.0 throughout.
Prompts are user-controlled, resources application-controlled, tools model-controlled.
Elicitation is the only current client feature; Sampling, Roots and Logging are deprecated in 2026-07-28.
Protocol version and client capabilities are required in `_meta` on every request; there is no `initialize`.
Unsupported version gives `-32022` with the supported list; servers must implement `server/discover`.

gotchas.trap: Negotiating capabilities once at connection time and caching them per socket.
gotchas.correct: In 2026-07-28 capabilities are sent with each request; a connection is not a session.

gotchas.trap: Using `clientInfo.name` to decide what a caller is allowed to do.
gotchas.correct: Client info is self-reported; authorization must come from verified credentials.

gotchas.trap: Treating a deprecated feature as already removed.
gotchas.correct: Deprecations run at least 12 months; plan the migration while the feature still works.

lessons.lab: Read the 2026-07-28 changelog and make a two-column table of features that were removed versus deprecated. Then write the `_meta` block a client would send on a `tools/call` request, and the `-32022` error a server that only supports an older version would return.

lessons.title: Transports: stdio, Streamable HTTP and the stateless model
lessons.summary: How MCP messages move over stdio and Streamable HTTP in the 2026-07-28 revision, which headers and status codes matter, how cancellation and streaming work, what was removed or deprecated, and how multi round-trip requests replace server-initiated calls.

sections.heading: stdio
sections.body:
With stdio the client launches the server as a **subprocess** and exchanges newline-delimited JSON-RPC over its standard input and output. Cancellation is a `notifications/cancelled` message.

Authorization on stdio should **not** follow the OAuth flow; the server takes credentials from its environment. Anything the server prints to stdout that is not a protocol message corrupts the stream, so diagnostics go to stderr.

Even over stdio, the spec is explicit that an open connection such as a stdio process is **not** a conversation or session. State that spans requests uses explicit identifiers passed on each request.

sections.heading: Streamable HTTP
sections.body:
A remote server exposes a single MCP endpoint that accepts **POST**:

- Every message is a new POST, with `Accept` listing both `application/json` and `text/event-stream`.
- A notification POST gets `202 Accepted` with no body.
- A request gets either a JSON response or a **request-scoped SSE stream**, which may carry `notifications/progress` (and log messages, if requested) before the final response. The server must not send requests on that stream.
- Headers: `MCP-Protocol-Version` must match the body or the server returns 400 (HeaderMismatch, `-32020`); `Mcp-Method` is sent on every request, and `Mcp-Name` on `tools/call`, `resources/read` and `prompts/get`, so gateways can route without parsing bodies.
- An unknown method gets 404 with `-32601`.

SSE responses should send `X-Accel-Buffering: no` so proxies do not buffer progress events.

sections.heading: Cancellation and broken streams
sections.body: On HTTP, **cancelling a request means closing its response stream**; there is no `notifications/cancelled` on HTTP. Resumability with `Last-Event-ID` was removed, so if a stream breaks the request is lost and the client must **re-issue it with a new JSON-RPC id**. Side-effecting tools should therefore be safe to retry.

sections.heading: What was removed and what was deprecated
sections.body:
Removed from Streamable HTTP in 2026-07-28: `Mcp-Session-Id`, the standalone GET stream, DELETE for ending sessions and `Last-Event-ID`. A modern-only server answers GET and DELETE with **405** and ignores session headers. The `ping` and `logging/setLevel` methods were removed.

Deprecated (still usable during the deprecation window): the old **HTTP+SSE** transport from 2024-11-05, Sampling, Roots, Logging and Dynamic Client Registration.

Change notifications now flow through **`subscriptions/listen`**: one long-lived POST whose response stream carries the notifications the client opted into (`toolsListChanged`, `promptsListChanged`, `resourcesListChanged`, `resourceSubscriptions`), each tagged with `io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId`. It replaces both the GET stream and `resources/subscribe`.

sections.heading: Multi round-trip requests replace server-initiated calls
sections.body:
A server can no longer send requests to the client. When a `tools/call`, `resources/read` or `prompts/get` needs more input, the server returns a result with `resultType: "input_required"`, listing input requests (for example `elicitation/create`) and an opaque `requestState`.

The client gathers the input and **retries the original request with a new JSON-RPC id**, echoing `requestState` exactly without inspecting it. The server must treat `requestState` as attacker-controlled: integrity-protect it (HMAC or AEAD) when it affects authorization or business logic, bind it to the principal, a short TTL and the original request, and, when a state must be consumed at most once (a refund, a redemption), enforce single use server-side. It must not ask for input types the client did not declare.

sections.heading: Transport security
sections.body: Streamable HTTP servers **must validate `Origin`** and reject an invalid one with 403, to block DNS-rebinding attacks from web pages. Local servers should bind to **127.0.0.1**, not 0.0.0.0. A tool parameter marked with `x-mcp-header` is mirrored into an `Mcp-Param-{Name}` header (Base64-encoded when not plain ASCII) for routing, so never mark a secret that way: headers end up in proxy and access logs.

keyPoints: stdio: client-launched subprocess, newline-delimited JSON-RPC, credentials from the environment, cancel with `notifications/cancelled`.
Streamable HTTP: one POST endpoint; notifications get 202; requests get JSON or a request-scoped SSE stream.
`MCP-Protocol-Version` must match the body; `Mcp-Method` on every request; `Mcp-Name` on tools/call, resources/read, prompts/get.
HTTP cancellation is closing the stream; broken streams are re-issued with a new id (no `Last-Event-ID`).
Sessions, GET stream and DELETE are removed; HTTP+SSE, Sampling, Roots, Logging and DCR are deprecated.
MRTR: `input_required` result plus opaque `requestState`, retried with a new id; validate `Origin`, bind locally to 127.0.0.1.

gotchas.trap: Storing per-user state keyed by `Mcp-Session-Id`.
gotchas.correct: Session IDs are gone; pass explicit identifiers on each request and keep state in a store.

gotchas.trap: Sending `notifications/cancelled` over HTTP.
gotchas.correct: On HTTP the client cancels by closing the response stream.

gotchas.trap: Resuming a dropped SSE stream with `Last-Event-ID`.
gotchas.correct: Resumability was removed; re-issue the request with a new JSON-RPC id.

gotchas.trap: Trusting `requestState` because the client echoed it back.
gotchas.correct: It is attacker-controlled; sign or encrypt it, bind it to principal and request, short TTL, single use.

lessons.lab: With curl, POST a `tools/call` to a local MCP endpoint twice: once with matching `MCP-Protocol-Version` header and body version, once with a mismatch. Then send a GET and a request with a foreign `Origin`. Record the status codes and compare them with the transport rules (400 HeaderMismatch, 405, 403).

lessons.title: Building an MCP server with the TypeScript SDK
lessons.summary: How to register tools with Zod schemas, return structured content and model-readable errors, report progress and honour cancellation in the TypeScript SDK, and why you must know which SDK line (v1 or v2) and which protocol revision your code targets.

sections.heading: Two SDK lines, two protocol eras
sections.body:
The TypeScript SDK now ships in two lines:

- **v1**, the `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` package, is the maintenance line. It implements the spec **up to 2025-11-25** and support for 2026-07-28 is not planned for it. Its API still has the `initialize` handshake, optional sessions and server-to-client requests.
- **v2** ships as separate packages, `@modelcontextprotocol/server` and `@modelcontextprotocol/client` (plus `/core` and framework adapters), and implements **2026-07-28**. It requires Zod 4 and Node 20 or later.

The code in this lesson is v1 code. The habits it teaches (schemas, structured output, error results, progress, cancellation) carry over to v2, but the wire behaviour described in the transport lesson is the 2026-07-28 behaviour that only v2 speaks. Always check which line a project depends on before reasoning about headers or sessions.

sections.heading: Registering a tool with Zod schemas
Structured content and output schemas
sections.body: When a tool declares an `outputSchema`, its `structuredContent` must conform to it. Clients can then validate and use the result programmatically. For backwards compatibility, also return the same JSON **serialised in a text content block**, because not every client reads `structuredContent`. Keep outputs small and use stable identifiers, since the result goes straight into the model's context.

sections.heading: Two kinds of error
sections.body:
MCP separates errors by who should handle them:

- **Protocol errors** (unknown tool, malformed request) are JSON-RPC errors, for example `-32602` "Unknown tool". They are for the client.
- **Tool execution errors** (an upstream API failed, a business rule rejected the input, a record was not found) are returned **in the result with `isError: true`** and a text explanation. Clients should pass these to the model so it can self-correct.

Write execution errors as instructions: say what went wrong and what to try next ("No order ord_missing. Use search_orders to find IDs."). Throwing a generic exception turns a recoverable situation into an opaque failure.

sections.heading: Progress and cancellation
sections.body:
If the caller included a `progressToken` in the request's `_meta`, the handler may send `notifications/progress` with that token, a `progress` value and an optional `total`. Only send progress when a token was supplied.

The handler's `extra.signal` is an `AbortSignal` that fires when the request is cancelled. Check it between steps and pass it to `fetch` and database drivers so abandoned work actually stops. On HTTP under 2026-07-28 the trigger is the client closing the stream; on stdio it is `notifications/cancelled`. In the SDK, cancellation reaches your handler through that abort signal, so honouring it covers both transports.

sections.heading: Transport wiring and local safety
sections.body:
In v1, `new StreamableHTTPServerTransport({ sessionIdGenerator: undefined, enableJsonResponse: true })` gives the nearest equivalent to stateless operation: no session IDs and plain JSON responses. The transport also accepts `allowedHosts`, `allowedOrigins` and `enableDnsRebindingProtection`; `createMcpExpressApp({ host: 'localhost' })` turns DNS-rebinding protection on.

In v2 the migration guide shows entry points such as `serveStdio(() => createServer())` and `createMcpHandler(() => createServer())`, with a fresh server built per request. Treat those names as illustrations from the migration guide and check the installed version's types before relying on them.

keyPoints: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` (v1) speaks protocol up to 2025-11-25; v2 (`@modelcontextprotocol/server` / `client`) implements 2026-07-28.
Use `registerTool` with Zod schemas; `tool()`/`resource()`/`prompt()` are deprecated.
Return `structuredContent` matching `outputSchema` and the same JSON as a text block.
Business and upstream failures: `isError: true` result with actionable text. Unknown tool or bad request: JSON-RPC error.
Send progress only when a `progressToken` was supplied; honour `extra.signal` for cancellation.

gotchas.trap: Throwing an exception when a record is not found.
gotchas.correct: Return `isError: true` with guidance so the model can recover.

gotchas.trap: Returning only `structuredContent`.
gotchas.correct: Also include the serialised JSON in a text block for clients that ignore structured output.

gotchas.trap: Assuming the v1 SDK speaks the 2026-07-28 stateless protocol.
gotchas.correct: v1 stops at 2025-11-25; use the v2 packages for the current revision.

gotchas.trap: Ignoring the abort signal in long handlers.
gotchas.correct: Check `extra.signal` and pass it to downstream calls so cancelled work stops.

lessons.lab: Implement the `get_order` tool above with SDK v1, plus a `search_orders` tool with pagination. Call `get_order` with a malformed ID (watch the SDK reject it) and with `ord_missing` (watch the model-readable error). Add a slow step and confirm that cancelling the request aborts it.

lessons.title: Authorization for remote MCP servers
lessons.summary: How a remote MCP server acts as an OAuth 2.1 resource server: discovery through protected resource metadata, client registration, PKCE, the resource indicator and token audience, scopes and step-up, and the rules that stop token passthrough and mix-up attacks.

sections.heading: Roles in MCP authorization
sections.body: Authorization is optional in MCP, but for HTTP transports the spec uses **OAuth 2.1**. The MCP server is an OAuth **resource server**: it validates access tokens; a separate (or co-located) **authorization server** issues them; the MCP client is the OAuth client. The standards involved include RFC 6750 (bearer tokens), RFC 8414 (AS metadata), RFC 8707 (resource indicators), RFC 9728 (protected resource metadata), RFC 9207 (issuer identification) and Client ID Metadata Documents. stdio servers should take credentials from the environment instead.

sections.heading: Discovery: from 401 to the authorization server
sections.body:
An unauthenticated request gets **401** with a challenge such as:

```http
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://mcp.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource", scope="files:read"
```

The client fetches the **Protected Resource Metadata** (RFC 9728). If the header is absent it tries `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/<path>` and then the root. The metadata **must** list `authorization_servers`. The client then fetches authorization server metadata (OAuth AS metadata, then OpenID configuration) and checks that the document's `issuer` equals the issuer it used to build the URL.

sections.heading: Client registration
sections.body: The client registers in priority order: a **pre-registered** client ID if it has one; otherwise a **Client ID Metadata Document** (CIMD), where the `client_id` is an HTTPS URL that serves the client's metadata and the AS advertises `client_id_metadata_document_supported`; otherwise **Dynamic Client Registration** (RFC 7591), now deprecated; otherwise ask the user. Credentials are stored per issuer.

sections.heading: PKCE, the resource parameter and issuer checks
sections.body:
- **PKCE** is mandatory with method `S256`. If the AS metadata has no `code_challenge_methods_supported`, the client must refuse to proceed.
- The **`resource` parameter** (RFC 8707) is required on both the authorization and token requests, carrying the canonical server URI (for example `https://mcp.example.com/mcp`, no fragment). Send it even if the AS ignores it; it lets the AS mint a token whose audience is this server.
- Before redeeming the code, the client must validate the **`iss`** response parameter (RFC 9207) against the recorded issuer. That defends against mix-up attacks, which PKCE alone does not.
- Redirect URIs must be localhost or HTTPS; public clients get refresh-token rotation.

sections.heading: Token validation and no passthrough
sections.body:
Clients send `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on **every** request and never put tokens in the query string. The server **must validate the token's audience** is itself; an invalid or expired token gets 401.

MCP servers **must not accept or transit any other tokens**. If your server calls a downstream API, it uses its own credentials or a token issued for that API, never the token the client sent. Passing a client's token through breaks audience separation and lets a token meant for one service act on another.

sections.heading: Scopes and step-up
sections.body: When a valid token lacks a scope, the server returns **403** with `error="insufficient_scope"` and should list **all** scopes the operation needs in one challenge. The client then re-authorizes, requesting the **union** of the scopes it already asked for and the newly challenged ones (asking only for the new ones would drop existing access), and retries only a few times. Servers should not include `offline_access` in their challenges. The tool list may legitimately differ by the authorization on a request, so a narrowly scoped token can see fewer tools.

keyPoints: MCP server = OAuth 2.1 resource server; discovery starts from a 401 pointing to protected resource metadata.
Protected resource metadata must list `authorization_servers`; check the AS metadata `issuer` matches.
Registration order: pre-registered, CIMD, DCR (deprecated), ask the user.
PKCE S256 is mandatory; no `code_challenge_methods_supported` means stop.
`resource` on authorize and token requests; server validates audience; no token passthrough.
401 = invalid/expired token; 403 `insufficient_scope` = step-up with the union of scopes.

gotchas.trap: Forwarding the client's bearer token to a downstream API.
gotchas.correct: Forbidden: MCP servers must not accept or transit other tokens. Use the server's own credentials for downstream calls.

gotchas.trap: Accepting any token signed by the right issuer.
gotchas.correct: Also validate the audience is this MCP server.

gotchas.trap: On step-up, requesting only the newly challenged scope.
gotchas.correct: Request the union of previous and new scopes.

gotchas.trap: Relying on PKCE to stop mix-up attacks.
gotchas.correct: Validate `iss` (RFC 9207) against the recorded issuer before redeeming the code.

lessons.lab: Draw the full sequence for a first `tools/call` against a protected server: 401 with `resource_metadata`, PRM fetch, AS metadata fetch with issuer check, CIMD registration, authorize with PKCE and `resource`, `iss` check, token request with `resource`, retry with bearer. Then add the 403 `insufficient_scope` branch and the scopes the client requests on step-up.

lessons.title: Operating MCP servers and exposing a product safely
lessons.summary: What it takes to run an MCP server that other people's agents will use: discovery and versioning, the registry, caching hints, rate limits and validation duties, logging without the deprecated logging feature, and the trust boundaries around tool metadata, request state and user input.

sections.heading: Discovery and versioning in production
sections.body: Every 2026-07-28 server must implement `server/discover`, which lets clients learn supported versions and capabilities before calling anything. Plan versions deliberately: return `-32022` with an accurate `supported` list, consider serving both eras on one endpoint during migration, and track deprecations, which last at least 12 months. Pin your documentation to a spec revision rather than to "latest".

sections.heading: The MCP Registry
sections.body: The official **MCP Registry** is in preview. It stores `server.json` metadata under **reverse-DNS names** (for example `io.github.user/server`) whose ownership is verified by GitHub, DNS or HTTP challenge. It is intended for **aggregators** (sub-registries and marketplaces) rather than for hosts to query directly, it does **not** support private servers, and it does **not** security-scan servers; that is delegated to the underlying package registries (npm, PyPI, Docker Hub) and to downstream aggregators. Listing a server proves namespace ownership, not safety.

sections.heading: Caching and list stability
sections.body: List and read results carry `ttlMs` and `cacheScope` (`public` or `private`), so clients and gateways know how long they may cache and whether a result is shared or per-user. Return `tools/list` in a **deterministic order** to improve LLM prompt-cache hit rates. The tool list must not vary per connection, though it may vary by the authorization on the request; use `private` scope when it does. Notify list changes through `subscriptions/listen` rather than silently changing tools.

sections.heading: Server duties: validation, access control, rate limits
sections.body:
The tools page puts four **musts** on servers: validate all tool inputs, enforce access control, **rate-limit tool invocations**, and sanitise outputs. Another agent can call your tools in a tight loop, so per-principal rate limits and clear `isError` messages (including when to retry) protect both your backend and the caller.

On the client side the spec recommends confirming sensitive operations, showing inputs before calling, validating results, setting timeouts and logging for audit. Clients that aggregate several servers should disambiguate tool names, for example with a server prefix, and should not rely on `serverInfo.name`, which is not guaranteed unique.

sections.heading: Logging and tracing
sections.body: Protocol-level logging is deprecated and `logging/setLevel` was removed. A server must not emit `notifications/message` unless the request set `io.modelcontextprotocol/logLevel`. For operations, log to **stderr** on stdio servers and use **OpenTelemetry** for remote ones. The `_meta` keys `traceparent`, `tracestate` and `baggage` are reserved for W3C trace context, so a trace can follow a request from the host through your server.

sections.heading: Trust boundaries when other agents call you
sections.body:
- **Self-reported metadata is not identity.** `clientInfo` and `serverInfo` must not drive security decisions; use verified tokens.
- **Tool annotations are hints.** A client should treat annotations such as `readOnlyHint` as untrusted unless the server is trusted; a server cannot make a destructive tool safe by labelling it.
- **`requestState` is attacker-controlled.** Sign or encrypt it, bind it to principal and request, short TTL, and enforce single use server-side when it must be consumed once.
- **Never collect secrets through form elicitation.** Passwords, API keys, tokens and payment credentials need URL mode, where the client shows the full URL, does not prefetch it and opens it in a context the model cannot read; `accept` means consent, not completion, and the server must check that the same user finished the flow.
- **Schemas can be attack surface.** Do not dereference network `$ref` by default, and bound composition keywords.
- **Keep secrets out of headers.** Do not mark secret parameters with `x-mcp-header`.

keyPoints: `server/discover` is required; return accurate `-32022` data; deprecations last at least 12 months.
MCP Registry (preview): reverse-DNS names with verified ownership, for aggregators, no private servers, no security scanning.
`ttlMs` + `cacheScope` on lists; deterministic `tools/list` order helps prompt caching.
Servers must validate inputs, enforce access control, rate-limit invocations and sanitise outputs.
Logging feature deprecated: stderr for stdio, OpenTelemetry for remote; trace context in reserved `_meta` keys.
Annotations, client info and `requestState` are untrusted; secrets go through URL-mode elicitation only.

gotchas.trap: Treating a registry listing as a security review.
gotchas.correct: The registry verifies namespace ownership only; scanning is delegated to package registries and aggregators.

gotchas.trap: Returning tools in hash-map order that changes between calls.
gotchas.correct: Return a deterministic order to keep prompt caches warm.

gotchas.trap: Emitting log notifications on every request.
gotchas.correct: Only when the request set `logLevel`; otherwise use stderr or OpenTelemetry.

gotchas.trap: Asking for an API key with a form elicitation.
gotchas.correct: Form mode must not request secrets; use URL mode.

lessons.lab: Write an operations checklist for publishing your product's MCP server: reverse-DNS name and verification method, `server/discover` response, supported versions, `ttlMs`/`cacheScope` per list, per-principal rate limits and the `isError` text for throttling, OpenTelemetry spans, and which inputs could ever need URL-mode elicitation.

lessons.title: The context window as a budget
lessons.summary: A large context window is not a licence to fill it. Treat tokens as a scarce budget, decide what earns a place, and lay the prompt out so that its stable part can be cached and its changing part stays small.

sections.heading: Why more context is not free
sections.body:
Context engineering is "the set of strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens" that the model sees at each step. Two pressures make it a budget problem rather than a capacity problem:

- **Context rot.** Recall degrades as the window grows. Anthropic's guidance puts it bluntly: "Every new token introduced depletes this budget". The goal is the *smallest set of high-signal tokens* that makes the desired behaviour likely.
- **Cost and latency.** Every request re-sends the whole prompt. A bloated prefix is paid for on every turn of an agent loop.

Current Claude models have a very large window (1M tokens on the current lineup), but that is a ceiling, not a target. An agent that "fits" 600k tokens of documents is usually worse than one that loads the three files it needs.

sections.heading: What earns a place in the window
sections.body:
A useful audit is to ask, for each block of context, *would the agent behave worse without it?*

| Usually earns its place | Usually does not |
|---|---|
| A system prompt at the right altitude | Every edge case written as an if-then rule |
| A few diverse, canonical examples | A long laundry list of examples |
| Tool definitions that do not overlap | Many near-duplicate tools with ambiguous boundaries |
| Lightweight references (paths, IDs, queries) | Whole files or result sets "just in case" |
| Recent, relevant tool results | Stale raw tool output from 40 turns ago |

Bloated tool sets are called out as a common failure mode: overlapping tools create "ambiguous decision points about which tool to use". Fewer, clearer tools save tokens *and* improve choices.

sections.heading: Ordering and cache-friendly layout
sections.body:
Claude prompt caching works on a **prefix**. The prefix order is fixed: `tools` → `system` → `messages`. A cache hit needs the prefix to be byte-identical up to the breakpoint, so the layout rule is simple: **stable first, volatile last**.

1. Tool definitions (keep them stable for the whole session).
2. The system prompt and long-lived reference material.
3. Earlier conversation turns.
4. The new user turn and fresh tool results.

Anything dynamic placed early, such as a timestamp, a request ID or a per-user greeting in the first line of the system prompt, changes the prefix and turns every request into a cache write. Put such values in the latest user message instead.

What invalidates which part:

- Changing **tool definitions** invalidates everything after them, which is the whole cache.
- Changing `tool_choice` or adding images invalidates the messages portion only.
- Changing thinking settings or effort invalidates the messages portion.

On OpenAI the same principle applies: keep the tool list stable and narrow the usable set with `allowed_tools` rather than removing tools, which preserves caching.

sections.heading: Prompt caching mechanics
sections.body:
Key facts for Claude (check the docs for current numbers, they change):

- Up to **4 cache breakpoints** per request, set with `cache_control`. Automatic caching is a single top-level `cache_control` and uses one slot.
- Default TTL is **5 minutes**, refreshed each time the entry is read. A 1-hour TTL exists at a higher write price.
- Writes cost more than base input (1.25x for 5 minutes, 2x for 1 hour). Reads cost a small fraction of base input, and the fraction depends on the model.
- There is a **minimum cacheable length** (512 tokens on the 5.x models, higher on older ones). Shorter prefixes are *silently* not cached: no error, just no cache tokens in `usage`.
- Each breakpoint looks back a limited number of block positions (20) for a previous entry.

Reading `usage`: total input = `cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens`, where `input_tokens` counts only the tokens *after* the last breakpoint. Dashboards that chart only `input_tokens` will under-report real input.

**Worked example.** A 50,000-token stable prefix, 2,000 new tokens per turn, 20 turns, on a model with $2/MTok input and 0.05x cache reads: without caching about $2.08; with one 5-minute write and 19 reads about $0.30, roughly 86% cheaper.

$$C = \frac{50000 \cdot 1.25 \cdot 2 + 19 \cdot 50000 \cdot 0.05 \cdot 2 + 20 \cdot 2000 \cdot 2}{10^6} \approx 0.30$$

keyPoints: Context is a budget: aim for the smallest set of high-signal tokens, because recall degrades as context grows (context rot).
A huge window is a ceiling, not a target; curating beats stuffing.
Claude caches a prefix in the order tools, system, messages; keep stable content first and volatile content last.
Changing tool definitions invalidates the whole cache; tool_choice, images, thinking and effort changes invalidate the messages part.
Prompts under the minimum cacheable length are silently not cached.
Total input = cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens.

gotchas.trap: Putting the current timestamp at the top of the system prompt for "freshness".
gotchas.correct: It changes the prefix on every request. Put dynamic values in the latest user turn so the stable prefix still hits the cache.

gotchas.trap: Adding and removing tools per turn to keep the list short.
gotchas.correct: That rewrites the start of the prefix and invalidates the whole cache. Keep the list stable and use deferral, tool search or allowed_tools-style restriction.

gotchas.trap: Reading input_tokens as the full prompt size.
gotchas.correct: With caching, input_tokens covers only the tokens after the last breakpoint; add the cache read and creation counts.

gotchas.trap: Assuming every cache read is "90% off".
gotchas.correct: The read multiplier depends on the model and changes over time; check the pricing table.

lessons.lab: Take an agent request you already send. Move every dynamic value (timestamps, IDs, user name) out of the tools and system blocks into the newest user message, add one cache_control breakpoint at the end of the system prompt, and send the same request twice within a minute. Confirm that the second response reports cache_read_input_tokens and compute total input from all three usage fields.
