flashcards.front: When should an agent eval check the trajectory rather than only the outcome?
flashcards.back: To enforce hard constraints, such as forbidden tools or a required order like verify before refund, and to measure efficiency. Do not use it to demand one fixed valid path.

flashcards.front: What does tool-call accuracy measure?
flashcards.back: Whether the agent chose the right tool and passed valid arguments grounded in the context rather than invented ones.

flashcards.front: Name the three kinds of grader and the main weakness of each.
flashcards.back: Code-based graders are brittle with open-ended output. Model-based (LLM judge) graders are non-deterministic and need calibration. Human graders are slow and expensive.

flashcards.front: What is position bias in an LLM judge, and how do you reduce it?
flashcards.back: In pairwise comparisons the verdict can flip when the two answers swap places. Judge both orders and aggregate the results (balanced position calibration).

flashcards.front: How do you calibrate an LLM judge?
flashcards.back: Have humans label a sample, measure how often the judge agrees with them, refine the rubric where they disagree, and re-check after any change to the judge prompt or model.

flashcards.front: pass@k versus pass^k?
flashcards.back: pass@k is the chance that at least one of k trials succeeds. pass^k is the chance that all k succeed. For unattended agents, pass^k shows consistency. At 0.75 per trial, pass^3 is about 0.42.

flashcards.front: How big should a first agent eval set be?
flashcards.back: Small and real. Anthropic's research system started with about 20 queries reflecting real usage, because early changes have large effects.

flashcards.front: Capability eval versus regression eval?
flashcards.back: A capability eval starts at a low pass rate and measures what the agent can do. A regression eval should pass near 100% and catches breakage. Saturated capability tasks graduate into the regression suite.

flashcards.front: A task fails 0% of the time across many trials and every model. What should you suspect first?
flashcards.back: A broken task or grader. Read the transcripts before concluding the agent cannot do it.

flashcards.front: Why keep a held-out eval set?
flashcards.back: If you tune prompts and tool descriptions against every task, you overfit to the eval and its score stops predicting real quality.

flashcards.front: How should CI gate on noisy agent evals?
flashcards.back: Run several trials, compare with the baseline on the same tasks using a standard error, and block when the drop is beyond the noise or a must-pass task fails.

flashcards.front: Where do the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions live now, and what is their status?
flashcards.back: In the open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai repository (docs/gen-ai/). Everything is at Development status.

flashcards.front: Which attribute identifies the model provider in current OTel GenAI conventions?
flashcards.back: gen_ai.provider.name (required), for example anthropic or openai. It replaces gen_ai.system.

flashcards.front: What is the span name and kind for a tool execution?
flashcards.back: execute_tool {gen_ai.tool.name}, kind INTERNAL, with gen_ai.tool.name required and gen_ai.tool.call.id to join it to the model output.

flashcards.front: OTel gen_ai.usage.input_tokens versus Anthropic usage.input_tokens?
flashcards.back: The OTel value SHOULD include cache read and cache write tokens. Anthropic's input_tokens counts only the tokens after the last cache breakpoint.

flashcards.front: Are prompt and response contents captured by default in OTel GenAI spans?
flashcards.back: No. gen_ai.input.messages, gen_ai.output.messages, the tool-call arguments and results and similar attributes are opt-in, because they can contain sensitive data.

flashcards.front: How is trace context carried across an MCP call?
flashcards.back: In _meta.traceparent, which the MCP specification reserves for this purpose.

flashcards.front: Roughly how many more tokens do agents and multi-agent systems use than chat?
flashcards.back: About 4x for agents and about 15x for multi-agent systems, according to Anthropic's research-system post.

flashcards.front: What does the Message Batches API trade for its discount?
flashcards.back: Latency. It is 50% off, but runs asynchronously, with most batches done within an hour and expiry at 24 hours. It stacks with caching.

flashcards.front: Which change invalidates the whole prompt cache?
flashcards.back: Changing the tool definitions, because tools come first in the prefix (tools, then system, then messages).

flashcards.front: What is the first cost lever Anthropic suggests before switching models?
flashcards.back: Tuning effort: "Tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models."

flashcards.front: Response has stop_reason max_tokens with a tool_use block. What do you do?
flashcards.back: Do not execute it, because it may be truncated. Retry with a larger max_tokens.

flashcards.front: What does stop_reason pause_turn mean, and how do you handle it?
flashcards.back: A server-side tool loop hit its iteration limit. Send the response back so the model continues, rather than treating it as final.

flashcards.front: At roughly what toolset size does Claude's tool selection start to degrade?
flashcards.back: Beyond about 30 to 50 tools. Use tool search with deferred loading, clearer descriptions and consolidated tools.

flashcards.front: Does strict: true stop hallucinated tool arguments?
flashcards.back: It stops schema-invalid arguments, such as missing fields or wrong types. It does not stop well-formed invented values, so validate IDs on the server and return instructive errors.

flashcards.front: What is context rot, and name two mitigations.
flashcards.back: Recall degrades as the context grows. Mitigations include compaction or clearing old tool results, notes kept outside the window, subagents with clean windows, and just-in-time loading.

flashcards.front: Direct vs indirect prompt injection
flashcards.back: Direct: the user tries to override the agent's instructions. Indirect: instructions are hidden in content the agent reads (pages, emails, tool results, retrieved chunks, tool descriptions).

flashcards.front: The "lethal trifecta" (term coined by Simon Willison)
flashcards.back: Private data + exposure to untrusted content + an exfiltration channel in one agent context. Remove at least one leg.

flashcards.front: Why are tool results untrusted input?
flashcards.back: The model cannot reliably tell data from instructions, and tool results often carry third-party content an attacker can control.

flashcards.front: OWASP LLM01 and LLM06 (2025)
flashcards.back: LLM01 Prompt Injection; LLM06 Excessive Agency.

flashcards.front: OWASP Agentic ASI01 and ASI06
flashcards.back: ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack; ASI06 Memory & Context Poisoning (Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026).

flashcards.front: What does CaMeL do against prompt injection?
flashcards.back: Derives control and data flow from the trusted user query so untrusted data cannot change program flow, and uses capabilities to block exfiltration (77% of AgentDojo tasks solved securely vs 84% undefended).

flashcards.front: OWASP LLM05 Improper Output Handling
flashcards.back: Model output is untrusted before it reaches a shell, SQL, HTML or another system: validate, escape and parameterise.

flashcards.front: MCP step-up after 403 insufficient_scope
flashcards.back: Request the union of previously requested and newly challenged scopes; retry only a few times; no wildcard scopes.

flashcards.front: What does effective sandboxing require (Anthropic, Claude Code)?
flashcards.back: Both filesystem and network isolation. Claude Code uses bubblewrap / seatbelt plus a domain-restricting proxy.

flashcards.front: Usability benefit Anthropic reports from sandboxing
flashcards.back: Permission prompts dropped by 84%, because actions inside the boundary no longer need case-by-case approval.

flashcards.front: Egress control for agents
flashcards.back: Route traffic through a proxy with a host allow-list and refuse URLs constructed from model output; this cuts the exfiltration leg.

flashcards.front: SSRF risk in MCP OAuth discovery
flashcards.back: A malicious server can point metadata at internal targets such as 169.254.169.254. Require HTTPS, block private/loopback/link-local ranges, validate redirects, use an egress proxy.

flashcards.front: Tool poisoning
flashcards.back: Malicious instructions hidden in a tool's description, annotations or schema. Descriptions and annotations are untrusted unless the server is trusted.

flashcards.front: Rug pull (MCP)
flashcards.back: A server changes tool definitions after approval. Pin a hash of approved definitions and re-review on list_changed or cache expiry.

flashcards.front: MCP confused deputy preconditions
flashcards.back: A proxy server using a static client ID with a third-party AS, dynamic registration, a consent cookie at the third-party AS, and no per-client consent.

flashcards.front: Token passthrough
flashcards.back: Forbidden: MCP servers MUST NOT accept or transit tokens not issued for them. It bypasses controls, breaks audit trails and makes the server an exfiltration proxy.

flashcards.front: How does an MCP server stop DNS rebinding?
flashcards.back: Validate the Origin header (invalid gets 403) and bind local servers to 127.0.0.1, not 0.0.0.0.

flashcards.front: One-click MCP server install rule
flashcards.back: Show the exact, untruncated command and require approval; run the server sandboxed and prefer stdio for local servers.

flashcards.front: MCP stance on human approval of tool calls
flashcards.back: There SHOULD always be a human in the loop able to deny tool invocations; clients SHOULD confirm sensitive operations, show inputs and log for audit.

flashcards.front: What should an agent audit log record?
flashcards.back: The acting user, tool name and arguments, result (or hash), approvals given, timestamps and a trace id linking to the model call.

flashcards.front: State handle hijacking (MCP 2026-07-28)
flashcards.back: A state handle is not authentication. Bind it server-side to the user id from the verified token, e.g. <user_id>:<handle>.

flashcards.front: Can form-mode elicitation request an API key?
flashcards.back: No. Form mode MUST NOT request passwords, API keys, tokens or payment credentials; use URL mode.

flashcards.front: Does the MCP Registry security-scan servers?
flashcards.back: No. It verifies namespace ownership (GitHub, DNS or HTTP challenge); security scanning is delegated elsewhere.

questions.scenario: A support platform receives tickets about billing, technical faults and refund requests. Each category needs a different prompt, a different tool set and, for refunds, a stricter model.
questions.stem: Which pattern fits this design best?
options: Orchestrator-workers, with the orchestrator inventing subtasks for each ticket
Routing: classify the ticket, then send it to a specialised handler
A fully autonomous agent with every tool from every category
Evaluator-optimiser, looping until a judge approves the reply
questions.explanation: Routing fits inputs that fall into distinct categories better handled separately. A classifier step sends each ticket to the prompt, tools and model for its category.
rationales: The subtasks are not unpredictable; the categories are known in advance, so a runtime planner adds cost without benefit.
Correct. Known, distinct categories with different handling are the textbook case for routing.
Giving one agent every tool increases confusion and cost and ignores that the categories are known.
Evaluator-optimiser is for iterative refinement against clear criteria, not for dispatching by category.

questions.scenario: A team translates product documentation. Reviewers have a written checklist (terminology list, tone, no untranslated strings), and a second pass that applies reviewer feedback reliably improves quality.
questions.stem: Which workflow pattern is the best fit?
options: Prompt chaining with no checks between steps
Parallelisation by voting across five translations
A multi-agent system with one sub-agent per paragraph
Evaluator-optimiser: one call translates, another evaluates against the checklist and feeds back
questions.explanation: Evaluator-optimiser fits when there are clear evaluation criteria and feedback measurably improves the result. Both conditions are stated in the scenario.
rationales: A plain chain would not use the checklist to drive iteration.
Voting picks among attempts but does not apply targeted feedback.
Per-paragraph sub-agents lose shared terminology context and multiply cost.
Correct. Clear criteria plus useful feedback is exactly when evaluator-optimiser pays off.

questions.scenario: A coding assistant receives feature requests. Some touch one file; others touch a dozen files whose identity is only known after reading the code.
questions.stem: Which pattern lets the system decide the subtasks per request?
options: Orchestrator-workers
Sectioning, with a fixed list of files per request type
Prompt chaining through a fixed sequence of five steps
Routing to one of three prewritten change templates
questions.explanation: Orchestrator-workers is for complex tasks where you cannot predict the subtasks needed. The orchestrator inspects the request and delegates work to workers at run time.
rationales: Correct. The number and identity of subtasks are only known at run time, which is the defining case.
Sectioning needs the parts fixed in advance, which the scenario rules out.
A fixed chain cannot adapt to a variable number of files.
Templates cannot cover changes whose shape depends on the codebase.

questions.scenario: An internal tool turns a meeting transcript into an action-item list, then drafts an email from that list. The steps never change, and the team wants to check that the list is not empty before drafting.
questions.stem: What is the simplest suitable design?
options: An autonomous agent that decides whether to draft the email
A lead agent with two sub-agents
Prompt chaining with a programmatic check between the two calls
Evaluator-optimiser with three refinement rounds
questions.explanation: The task decomposes cleanly into fixed subtasks, which is the case for prompt chaining. Code can check the intermediate output before the next call.
rationales: An agent adds unpredictability to a fixed two-step task.
Sub-agents add tokens and coordination for no gain here.
Correct. Two fixed steps with a check in between is a textbook chain.
Nothing in the scenario calls for iterative refinement.

questions.scenario: A product manager asks for an "autonomous agent" to extract five fields from supplier invoices. The invoices share a format, latency must stay under two seconds, and every extraction must be auditable step by step.
questions.stem: What should the engineer recommend?
options: Build an agent with a large tool set so it can handle future formats
Start with a single call or a short fixed workflow with validation, and add complexity only if measurement shows a gap
Use a multi-agent system so each field has its own sub-agent
Build an agent but hide its intermediate steps to keep the output clean
questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance is to find the simplest solution and increase complexity only when needed. A known, fixed task with tight latency and audit needs favours a plain workflow over an agent.
rationales: Designing for hypothetical future formats adds cost and unpredictability now.
Correct. Simple, measurable and auditable meets every stated constraint.
Five sub-agents would multiply tokens and latency for a fixed extraction.
Hiding steps works against the transparency principle and the audit requirement.

questions.scenario: A security team wants an LLM review of each pull request for vulnerabilities. Missing a real issue is costly, so they want more confidence than one pass gives.
questions.stem: Which variant of parallelisation fits?
options: Sectioning, splitting the diff into halves reviewed once each
Prompt chaining, reviewing the diff and then summarising
Routing the diff to one reviewer prompt by language
Voting: run several independent reviews and combine their flags
questions.explanation: Voting runs the same task several times to gain confidence in the result. Sectioning is about speed through independent parts, not confidence.
rationales: Sectioning speeds up work but each part is still reviewed only once.
A chain does not add independent judgments.
Routing picks one handler; it does not add confidence.
Correct. Multiple independent attempts are the voting variant.

questions.stem: Which TWO conditions best justify moving from a workflow to an agent? (Select two.)
options: The number of steps needed cannot be predicted in advance
The task decomposes cleanly into fixed subtasks
A simpler design has been tried and measured, and it does not meet the bar
The team wants the system to appear more advanced to stakeholders
questions.explanation: Agents fit open-ended problems where the required number of steps is hard or impossible to predict. The guidance is also to increase complexity only when simpler solutions fall short.
rationales: Correct. Unpredictable step counts are the core reason to give the model control flow.
Fixed subtasks point to prompt chaining, not an agent.
Correct. Complexity should be added only when the simpler design is shown to fall short.
Appearance is not an engineering reason and adds cost and risk.

questions.scenario: An agent loop on Claude stops whenever the response contains any text block. Users report the agent often says "Let me check the database" and then ends without checking.
questions.stem: What is the correct fix?
options: Lower max_tokens so the model writes less text
Tell the model in the system prompt never to write text before a tool call
Branch on stop_reason and keep looping while it is "tool_use"
Run every tool after every response whether or not the model asked
questions.explanation: A Claude response can contain text and tool_use blocks together. The loop should branch on stop_reason and continue while it is tool_use, running the requested tools and returning their results.
rationales: Fewer tokens can truncate output and does not fix the control-flow bug.
Prompting around a loop bug is fragile; text before a tool call is normal.
Correct. stop_reason is the signal for whether the model wants tools run.
Running unrequested tools wastes calls and produces results for calls that never happened.

questions.scenario: In production logs, a long-running agent sometimes ends a turn with stop_reason "max_tokens" while writing a large tool_use input. The loop treats this like end_turn and returns the partial text to the user.
questions.stem: How should the loop handle this case?
options: Treat it as incomplete: do not execute the cut-off tool call, and retry with a higher output limit or handle the truncation explicitly
Execute the partial tool call with whatever arguments parsed
Treat it as success because the model chose to stop
Switch to temperature 0 so the output is shorter
questions.explanation: max_tokens means output was cut off at the limit, so the tool call is incomplete. The loop should not run a truncated call and should either raise the limit or handle the partial output deliberately.
rationales: Correct. Truncated output is not a finished turn.
Running a call with partial arguments can cause wrong side effects.
The model did not choose to stop; it hit the output limit.
Sampling settings do not fix truncation, and on API version 2026-10-21 sending temperature returns a 400.

questions.scenario: An agent with a web search tool occasionally loops for hundreds of turns on vague queries, running up large bills. The model never returns end_turn in those runs.
questions.stem: What is the most reliable control?
options: Add "stop when you are done" to the system prompt
Raise max_tokens so the model can finish its reasoning in one turn
Remove the search tool after the first call
Enforce a step cap and a cumulative token budget in the loop, with a defined outcome when hit
questions.explanation: Iteration and token budgets are client-side policy. The model's stop signal is not a budget, so the loop must enforce caps and decide what happens when they are reached.
rationales: A prompt instruction does not guarantee termination.
A larger output limit does nothing to cap the number of turns.
Changing tool definitions mid-run invalidates the prompt cache and breaks legitimate multi-search tasks.
Correct. Hard caps in code bound cost no matter what the model does.

questions.scenario: An agent completes a task in 20 sequential steps. Each step independently succeeds 95% of the time.
questions.stem: What is the approximate end-to-end success rate, and what does it imply?
options: About 95%, so no further checks are needed
About 36%, so add checks or verification between steps
About 82%, so the design is acceptable
About 5%, so the task cannot be automated
questions.explanation: Independent per-step success compounds as p to the 20th power, and 0.95^20 is about 0.36. Long runs need verification between steps, not only at the end.
rationales: Per-step reliability is not end-to-end reliability.
Correct. 0.95^20 ≈ 0.358, so errors compound quickly.
About 82% is the result for 0.99 per step, not 0.95.
5% is the per-step failure rate, not the run success rate.

questions.stem: Which TWO controls belong in the client-side agent loop as run policy? (Select two.)
options: A maximum number of model or tool calls per run
Sending temperature 0 on every request so the loop converges
A cumulative token or cost budget checked after each response
Removing tool definitions after the first turn to save tokens
questions.explanation: Step caps and token or cost budgets are policies the client enforces in the loop. Neither sampling settings nor removing tools bounds the run safely.
rationales: Correct. A step cap stops runaway loops.
Sampling does not make loops terminate, and on API version 2026-10-21 temperature returns a 400 even at its default.
Correct. A running budget from usage fields bounds spend.
Removing tools breaks later steps that need them and invalidates the prompt cache.

questions.scenario: A question-answering agent answers multi-hop questions from memory and often states wrong facts confidently. The team can give it a search tool.
questions.stem: Which reasoning pattern most directly addresses this?
options: Chain-of-thought only, with longer reasoning before answering
Reflexion with no external tools
ReAct: interleave reasoning with search actions and reason over each observation
Majority voting over several memory-only answers
questions.explanation: ReAct interleaves reasoning traces with actions, so the model grounds each step in observations from tools. Reasoning alone cannot correct facts the model does not have.
rationales: More reasoning without new information can still produce made-up facts.
Reflexion without a feedback signal or tools has nothing to correct against.
Correct. Acting on search results grounds the reasoning.
Voting over the same memory tends to repeat the same errors.

questions.scenario: A coding agent fails hidden unit tests on its first attempt. The team cannot fine-tune the model but can run several attempts per task and store text between them.
questions.stem: Which approach matches Reflexion?
options: Fine-tune on failed attempts overnight
After each failure, have the agent write a verbal self-reflection, store it in episodic memory and include it in the next attempt
Increase sampling randomness and retry until a test passes
Discard failed attempts and retry with the same prompt
questions.explanation: Reflexion uses verbal self-reflection stored in an episodic memory buffer, with no weight updates. The test failures provide the feedback signal that the reflection uses.
rationales: Reflexion changes no weights.
Correct. Reflections in memory carry lessons into the next attempt.
Random retries ignore what went wrong.
Retrying the same prompt with no memory learns nothing.

questions.scenario: A team upgrades an agent to Claude Opus 5.5. Their request sets thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: 16000} to make planning steps deeper.
questions.stem: What should they do?
options: Raise budget_tokens to 64000 for harder tasks
Remove thinking and use temperature to control depth
Keep the setting; it is the current way to control reasoning
Drop the manual budget and steer adaptive thinking with the effort parameter
questions.explanation: Manual budget_tokens thinking is deprecated on Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 and not accepted on later models. Current models use adaptive thinking, steered by effort.
rationales: A larger budget is still the unsupported control.
Temperature is not a reasoning-depth control and sending it returns a 400 on API version 2026-10-21.
This is legacy configuration on current models.
Correct. effort is the lever on current models.

questions.scenario: A data-migration agent runs 30 expensive, mostly predictable steps. A human must review the approach before anything runs, and the team wants fewer calls to the most capable model.
questions.stem: Which design fits best?
options: Plan-and-execute: produce an explicit plan for review, run steps with a cheaper executor, and replan on failure
Pure ReAct with the capable model deciding every step
Evaluator-optimiser over the final migration report
A single call that outputs all 30 migration scripts with no review
questions.explanation: Plan-and-execute makes the plan visible up front, which supports review and the transparency principle. Executors can be cheaper, and replanning handles failures.
rationales: Correct. A reviewable plan plus cheaper execution matches all three needs.
Step-by-step ReAct gives no plan to review before acting and uses the capable model every step.
Judging the final report is too late to stop a bad migration.
One unreviewed call ignores the review requirement and offers no recovery.

questions.scenario: A pipeline uses Claude for a quick routing step and a separate hard planning step. Both currently use the same model settings, and the routing step is too slow.
questions.stem: Which change is most appropriate?
options: Use a lower effort for the routing step and a higher effort for the planning step
Set budget_tokens to 0 for routing
Add a stop sequence to the planning step
Send both steps in one request to share thinking
questions.explanation: On current Claude models, effort steers how much adaptive thinking is used. Simple, latency-sensitive steps can run at lower effort, while hard planning benefits from more.
rationales: Correct. Match effort to the difficulty of each step.
budget_tokens is not accepted on current models.
A stop sequence does not change reasoning depth or speed up routing.
Merging the steps removes the separation that makes each easy to tune and test.

questions.scenario: A team proposes five parallel sub-agents to refactor a module, one per file. Every file's changes depend on interface decisions made in the others.
questions.stem: What is the best advice?
options: Add more sub-agents so each function gets its own
Use one agent that holds the whole module in context, since the work has shared context and tight dependencies
Keep five sub-agents but forbid them from reading other files
Use voting across five full refactors and merge them
questions.explanation: Anthropic notes multi-agent systems are a poor fit for tasks that need shared context or have many dependencies between agents, citing most coding work. One agent with the whole picture avoids conflicting decisions.
rationales: More agents make inconsistent interface decisions more likely.
Correct. Shared, dependent work favours a single agent.
Isolation makes the dependency problem worse.
Merging five independent refactors creates conflicts, not consensus.

questions.scenario: In a research agent, each sub-agent returns all the raw pages it read, about 50,000 tokens each. The lead agent's quality drops as runs progress.
questions.stem: What change best restores the benefit of sub-agents?
options: Give the lead a larger output limit
Merge all sub-agents into the lead
Have each sub-agent return a condensed summary, on the order of 1,000 to 2,000 tokens
Ask sub-agents to return raw pages only for the first half of the run
questions.explanation: Sub-agents give context isolation by exploring in clean windows and returning condensed summaries, often around 1,000 to 2,000 tokens. Raw dumps flood the lead's context and cause context rot.
rationales: Output limits do not address an overloaded input context.
That removes isolation entirely and makes the problem worse.
Correct. Condensed results keep the lead's context focused.
Raw dumps at any stage still flood the lead's context.

questions.scenario: A team considers a multi-agent design for two workloads: (A) answering simple FAQ lookups at high volume, and (B) occasional, high-value market research spanning many independent sources.
questions.stem: Which decision is best supported by Anthropic's findings?
options: Use multi-agent for both, since it beat single-agent by 90.2%
Use multi-agent for A only, because volume justifies parallelism
Use a single agent for both, because multi-agent never helps
Use multi-agent for B only, since it uses about 15x chat tokens and pays off on high-value, parallelisable tasks
questions.explanation: Multi-agent systems use about 15 times the tokens of chat and pay off on high-value tasks with breadth that can be explored in parallel. Simple lookups should use one agent with few tool calls.
rationales: The 90.2% result was on an internal research eval and does not justify the cost for simple lookups.
High volume of simple work multiplies the token overhead.
Multi-agent did help on research-style tasks.
Correct. Match the token cost to task value and parallel breadth.

questions.stem: A long multi-agent research run fails at step 37 when a tool times out. Which TWO practices match what Anthropic describes for reliability? (Select two.)
options: Resume from a saved checkpoint instead of restarting the run
Restart the whole run from scratch so state is clean
Combine retry logic with letting the agent adapt when a tool fails
Make every sub-agent batch synchronous so the lead waits for all results
questions.explanation: Because errors compound in stateful agents, the research system resumes from checkpoints and pairs retries with the agent's ability to adapt. Synchronous batches are named as a bottleneck, not a fix.
rationales: Correct. Checkpoints avoid repeating expensive work.
Restarting wastes completed work and money.
Correct. Retries plus adaptation handle transient and persistent failures.
Synchronous batches slow the system and do not improve reliability.

questions.scenario: In a two-agent system, a planner hands work to an executor by writing a prose recap in chat. Details such as file names and IDs get lost or paraphrased across hand-offs.
questions.stem: Which change most improves the hand-off?
options: Ask the planner to write longer recaps
Keep shared state in durable structured notes outside the context window and pass references to them
Merge both agents' full transcripts into each request
Have the executor ask the planner to repeat itself when unsure
questions.explanation: Structured note-taking outside the context window is a long-horizon technique that keeps state durable and exact. Passing references avoids lossy retelling.
rationales: Longer prose is still a lossy copy.
Correct. Durable notes keep exact details and keep context small.
Full transcripts bloat context and degrade recall.
Extra round trips add cost and still rely on paraphrase.

questions.scenario: An agent connected to several MCP servers can delete records and send external emails. Today it runs every tool call automatically. One server marks its delete tool with destructiveHint: false.
questions.stem: Which design best follows the MCP tools guidance?
options: Trust the annotation and auto-run the delete tool
Remove the human from the loop to reduce latency
Only log tool calls after they run
Require user confirmation for sensitive operations, showing the tool inputs first, and do not rely on untrusted annotations alone
questions.explanation: The MCP spec says a human SHOULD be able to deny tool invocations and that clients should confirm sensitive operations and show inputs first. Annotations are untrusted unless the server is trusted.
rationales: Annotations from an untrusted server cannot be relied on.
That removes the safeguard the spec recommends.
After-the-fact logs do not let anyone deny a harmful call.
Correct. A risk-based approval gate with visible inputs is the recommended control.

questions.scenario: An MCP server on revision 2026-07-28 needs the user to choose a shipping option partway through a tools/call.
questions.stem: How does the protocol handle this?
options: The server sends elicitation/create to the client over a GET stream
The server returns an input_required result; the client collects the answer and retries the call with a new JSON-RPC id, inputResponses and the echoed requestState
The server holds the HTTP response open and resumes it later with Last-Event-ID
The client opens a session with Mcp-Session-Id so the server can remember the call
questions.explanation: 2026-07-28 removes server-initiated requests and uses Multi Round-Trip Requests. The server returns an InputRequiredResult and the client retries with a new id, inputResponses and requestState echoed exactly.
rationales: The GET stream and server-to-client requests were removed in this revision.
Correct. This is the MRTR flow.
SSE resumability with Last-Event-ID was removed.
Mcp-Session-Id was removed; the protocol is stateless.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about requestState in MCP Multi Round-Trip Requests are correct? (Select two.)
options: The client may edit requestState to record the user's choice
The server must treat requestState as attacker-controlled and integrity-protect it when it affects authorisation or business logic
The client must echo requestState exactly and never inspect it
The retry must reuse the original JSON-RPC id so the server can match it
questions.explanation: The client echoes requestState unchanged and does not inspect it, and the retry uses a new JSON-RPC id. The server must treat it as attacker-controlled, protect it with HMAC or AEAD where it affects authorisation or business logic, and should bind it to the principal, a short TTL and the originating request.
rationales: The user's answer goes in inputResponses; the client must not change requestState.
Correct. requestState comes back through the client and can be tampered with.
Correct. It is opaque to the client.
The retry must use a new JSON-RPC id.

questions.scenario: An agent starts a report job on an MCP server that takes about 40 minutes. Network drops sometimes break the HTTP response stream, and the job is lost.
questions.stem: Which approach gives a durable, resumable run under 2026-07-28?
options: Use the Tasks extension: get a task handle, poll with tasks/get and send input with tasks/update
Reconnect with Last-Event-ID to resume the stream
Keep a GET stream open for the server to push the result
Retry the same request with the same JSON-RPC id after each drop
questions.explanation: The Tasks extension gives a durable handle for long-running work that the client can poll and update. In 2026-07-28 a broken stream loses the request, and SSE resumability was removed.
rationales: Correct. A task handle survives dropped connections.
Last-Event-ID resumability was removed.
The GET stream was removed.
A lost request must be re-issued with a new id, and that would restart the job, not resume it.

questions.scenario: During a run, an MCP server needs the user's API key for a third-party service and plans to collect it with a form-mode elicitation.
questions.stem: What should happen instead?
options: Use form mode but mark the field as a password
Ask the model to request the key in its reply text
Use URL mode, so the user enters the key in a context the client and model cannot inspect
Store the key in requestState for later calls
questions.explanation: Form-mode elicitation must not request passwords, API keys, tokens or payment credentials. Those flows use URL mode, which the client opens in a context neither it nor the model can inspect.
rationales: Form mode must not be used for secrets at all.
That puts the secret into the model's context.
Correct. URL mode is for sensitive input.
requestState passes through the client and is attacker-controlled, so it is no place for secrets.

questions.scenario: CRM assistant
questions.stem: A CRM agent has a `list_contacts` tool that returns all 5,000 contacts. To answer "What is Dana Ortiz's phone number?" the agent pages through results, uses most of its context and sometimes reports the wrong Dana. What is the best tool change?
options: Raise the model's context budget so the full list fits in one call
Return the list as compact CSV instead of JSON
Add a system-prompt rule telling the agent to read the list carefully
Replace it with a `search_contacts` tool that takes a query and returns a small set of matches
questions.explanation: Anthropic's tool guidance is to build task-shaped tools rather than wrap list endpoints: a search tool does the filtering where it is cheap and returns only relevant rows. More context or a prompt rule leaves the agent reading thousands of rows, and a denser format only shrinks the same problem.
rationales: A bigger budget still makes the agent read every contact to find one.
Compact formats reduce tokens a little but keep the wrong tool shape.
Instructions do not remove the need to scan 5,000 rows.
Correct. Search beats list; the tool returns what the task needs.

sources.title: Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: GitHub agent
questions.stem: An agent exposes 40 thin GitHub tools, including `create_pr`, `review_pr`, `merge_pr` and `close_pr`. Transcripts show it often picks a near-duplicate tool. Which change follows the Claude tool-definition guidance?
options: Consolidate related PR operations into one namespaced tool with an `action` parameter
Shorten every description to one line so the model can compare them faster
Add more tools for each PR state so every case has an exact match
Force the correct tool with `tool_choice` on each turn
questions.explanation: The Claude docs recommend consolidating related operations into fewer tools, for example one tool with an action parameter, and using meaningful namespacing. Fewer, clearer tools reduce wrong selections. Forcing a tool assumes the app already knows the answer and is rejected on several current models.
rationales: Correct. Consolidation with an action parameter is the documented pattern.
The docs ask for more detailed descriptions, not shorter ones.
More near-duplicates make selection worse.
Forcing requires knowing the right tool in advance and returns 400 on several current Claude models.

questions.scenario: Ticketing tool
questions.stem: A `assign_ticket` tool has a parameter named `user`. The agent sometimes passes an email, sometimes a display name and sometimes an id, and the call fails. What is the most direct fix?
options: Retry the call automatically until it succeeds
Accept any of the three and guess which one was meant
Rename it to `user_id` and describe the expected id format in the schema and description
Remove the parameter and assign tickets to the caller
questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance is to use unambiguous parameter names such as user_id rather than user, and the Claude docs ask descriptions to state what each parameter means. Guessing hides errors and retries without a clearer contract repeat them.
rationales: Retries without a clearer contract repeat the same mistake.
Guessing can assign the ticket to the wrong person silently.
Correct. A precise name and documented format remove the ambiguity.
That breaks the tool's purpose.

sources.title: Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: Tool definitions review
questions.stem: You are reviewing tool definitions for a Claude agent. Which two practices match the Claude documentation? (Select two.)
options: Write descriptions of at least three to four sentences covering what the tool does, when to use it, its parameters and its limitations
Keep descriptions to a single short line and put usage rules in the system prompt instead
Make every `input_examples` entry valid against the tool's input schema
Include one deliberately invalid `input_examples` entry to show the model what to avoid
questions.explanation: The Claude docs ask for extremely detailed descriptions, at least three to four sentences on what, when, parameters and limitations. Input examples must validate against the schema; an invalid one makes the request return 400.
rationales: Correct. This is the documented description standard.
Descriptions are the main lever on tool selection; one line is too little.
Correct. Each example must be schema-valid.
An invalid example causes a 400 rather than teaching the model anything.

questions.scenario: MCP bridge
questions.stem: A team bridges an MCP server into the Claude Messages API by copying each MCP tool definition directly into `tools`. Requests fail with a 400 that points at the tool named `admin.tools.list`. What is the cause?
options: MCP tools cannot be used with the Messages API at all
Claude tool names must match `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$`, so the dots must be mapped to an allowed character
The tool is missing an `outputSchema`, which Claude requires
Tool names longer than 16 characters are rejected
questions.explanation: MCP tool names may contain dots, but Claude tool names must match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$. The bridge must rename such tools, for example to admin_tools_list, and map calls back. Output schemas are optional and the length limit is 128.
rationales: MCP tools can be bridged; the name format is the problem.
Correct. Dots are allowed in MCP names but not in Claude names.
outputSchema is an optional MCP field, not a Claude requirement.
The limit is 128 characters.

questions.scenario: Five MCP servers
questions.stem: An agent connects GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Grafana and Splunk MCP servers. Tool definitions consume tens of thousands of tokens on every request and the agent increasingly calls the wrong tool. What does the Claude documentation recommend?
options: Cache the tool block and keep loading every definition into the model's view
Split the agent into five agents, one per server, and pick one at random
Remove all tool descriptions to save tokens
Use the tool search tool and mark most tools `defer_loading: true` so only matching tools are loaded
questions.explanation: The tool search docs describe exactly this setup and say tool search typically cuts the definition tokens by over 85 percent, loading only a few relevant tools. They also note selection quality degrades past roughly 30 to 50 tools, so caching alone does not fix wrong picks.
rationales: Caching reduces cost but the model still sees too many tools to choose well.
Random routing does not solve selection.
Descriptions are what the model uses to choose; removing them makes things worse.
Correct. Deferred loading plus search addresses both tokens and selection accuracy.

questions.scenario: Tool search rollout
questions.stem: To minimise tokens, an engineer sets `defer_loading: true` on every tool, including the tool search tool, and adds `cache_control` to several deferred tools. Requests now fail. Which fix addresses both errors?
options: Keep at least one tool non-deferred, and remove `cache_control` from tools that use `defer_loading`
Switch from the BM25 variant to the regex variant
Stop sending deferred tool definitions in the request
Set `tool_choice` to `none` until the search runs
questions.explanation: The tool search docs require at least one non-deferred tool, otherwise the request returns 400, and defer_loading cannot be combined with cache_control. Deferred definitions are still sent on every request; deferral only controls what the model sees.
rationales: Correct. Both are documented 400 conditions.
The variant does not change either rule.
You still send every definition; deferral is not omission.
Disabling tools prevents the search itself.

questions.scenario: Agent loop bug
questions.stem: After Claude returns a `tool_use` block, the app sends a user message whose content is a text block, "Here is the result:", followed by the `tool_result`. The API returns 400. What is wrong?
options: Tool results must be sent with the `assistant` role
Tool results must be sent in the system prompt
The `tool_result` block must come first in the user content; text may only follow it
Text is never allowed in a message that carries tool results
questions.explanation: The Claude docs require tool_result blocks to come first in the user message content, with any text after them. Text before a tool_result is rejected. Results use the user role, and text after them is allowed.
rationales: Results go in a user message.
The system prompt is not where results go, and untrusted content should stay in tool_result blocks.
Correct. Order matters: results first, then text.
Text is allowed after the results.

questions.scenario: Parallel weather lookups
questions.stem: Claude requests `get_weather` for Paris and Tokyo in one turn. The app replies with two consecutive user messages, one `tool_result` each. What should it do instead?
options: Return only the first result and let Claude ask again for the second
Send both `tool_result` blocks in a single user message, each with its `tool_use_id`
Merge both results into one text block without ids
Send each result as a new assistant message
questions.explanation: All results for one assistant turn go in a single user message, one tool_result per tool_use_id, immediately after that turn. Dropping one leaves a request unanswered, and dropping ids loses the pairing.
rationales: Every tool_use in the turn needs a result.
Correct. Parallel results share one user message.
The ids are how results are matched to calls.
Results are user content, not assistant turns.

questions.scenario: Forced extraction
questions.stem: A pipeline on Claude Opus 5.5 sets `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "record_invoice"}` to guarantee schema-shaped output, and now every request returns 400. What is the documented fix?
options: Retry with exponential backoff
Switch to `tool_choice: any`
Enable manual extended thinking with a token budget
Use `tool_choice: auto` with `strict: true` on the tool, or use structured outputs
questions.explanation: On several current Claude models, including Opus 5.5 at the time of writing, forced tool_choice (any or tool) returns 400. The define-tools page points to auto plus strict: true, or structured outputs when only a JSON answer is needed. Retrying cannot fix a validation error, and manual thinking also blocks forcing.
rationales: A 400 is a request error, not a transient failure.
any is also a forced choice and is rejected the same way.
Manual thinking blocks forced tool use, and budget-style thinking is not accepted on current models.
Correct. This is the documented replacement.

questions.scenario: OpenAI strict mode
questions.stem: An OpenAI function has `strict: true` and a schema where `notes` is an optional string left out of `required`. The API rejects the schema. How should it be written?
options: List `notes` in `required` with type `["string", "null"]`, and set `additionalProperties: false` on the object
Remove `strict`; strict mode never supports optional data
Set `additionalProperties: true` so extra fields are allowed
Give `notes` a default value instead of listing it
questions.explanation: OpenAI strict mode requires additionalProperties: false on every object and every field in required; optional fields are expressed as nullable types. Allowing additional properties violates strict mode, and defaults do not replace the required list.
rationales: Correct. Required plus nullable is the strict-mode pattern.
Optional data is supported through nullable types.
Strict mode needs additionalProperties: false.
A default does not satisfy the every-field-required rule.

questions.scenario: Ordered side effects
questions.stem: An agent must call `create_branch` and then `commit_files` to that branch. Claude sometimes requests both in the same turn and the commit fails because the branch does not exist yet. What is the cleanest fix?
options: Merge the tools' results into one text block
Run all tool calls in random order and retry failures
Set `tool_choice: {"type": "auto", "disable_parallel_tool_use": true}`
Remove `commit_files` from the tool list
questions.explanation: When calls depend on each other's side effects, disable parallel tool use so Claude requests at most one tool per turn. The Claude docs show this as tool_choice: {"type": "auto", "disable_parallel_tool_use": true}. Random ordering and retries hide the dependency instead of respecting it.
rationales: Result formatting does not change call order.
Retries waste turns and can leave partial state.
Correct. Sequential calls preserve the dependency.
The agent still needs to commit files.

questions.scenario: Porting to OpenAI Responses
questions.stem: You are porting a tool loop to the OpenAI Responses API. Which two steps are correct? (Select two.)
options: Parse each `function_call` item's `arguments`, which arrive as a JSON string
Reply with a `function_call_output` item carrying the same `call_id` and an `output` string
Send tool results as an ordinary user text message describing what happened
Drop reasoning items from the next request to save tokens
questions.explanation: OpenAI function calls carry arguments as a JSON string and are answered with function_call_output items matched by call_id. The guide also says reasoning items must be passed back with tool outputs, so dropping them is wrong.
rationales: Correct. arguments is a string you must parse.
Correct. call_id pairs the output with the call.
Plain text loses the call pairing the API expects.
Reasoning items should be passed back with the outputs.

questions.scenario: Server tools in the loop
questions.stem: An agent uses Claude's web search server tool alongside client tools. The loop executes every tool call block it finds, and for a block with an id starting `srvtoolu_` it sends back a `tool_result`, which the API rejects. What should the loop do?
options: Execute web search locally and return the results as a `tool_result`
Return `tool_result` blocks only for client `tool_use` blocks; server tool calls run at Anthropic, which supplies their results
Remove the web search tool because it cannot be combined with client tools
Send the server tool result in the system prompt
questions.explanation: Server tools such as web search, web fetch, code execution and tool search run on Anthropic's infrastructure, and Anthropic supplies their results (usually in the same response; when a server call shares a parallel batch with client calls, its result can arrive in a later response). The Claude docs say never to return a tool_result for a srvtoolu_ id. Your code executes, and answers, only client tool_use blocks.
rationales: The server already ran the search; a client result for that id is invalid.
Correct. Only client tools are executed and answered by your code.
Server and client tools can be mixed.
That is not how results are returned, and untrusted content should not go in the system prompt.

questions.scenario: Flaky upstream API
questions.stem: A `get_invoice` tool calls an upstream API that sometimes rate-limits. Today the tool throws an exception and the whole agent run aborts. What is the better design?
options: Return the raw HTTP 429 response body with no explanation
Return an empty successful result so the agent keeps going
Remove the tool whenever the upstream API is unhealthy
Return a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` and a message such as "Rate limit exceeded. Retry after 60 seconds."
questions.explanation: The Claude docs mark execution failures with is_error: true and ask for instructive error messages, so the model can wait, retry or choose another path. An empty success misleads the model, and a raw status code gives it nothing to act on.
rationales: A raw 429 body is not actionable guidance.
A fake success leads to confident wrong answers.
Changing the tool list mid-run is disruptive and hides the cause.
Correct. Errors are results the model can act on.

questions.scenario: Project search
questions.stem: A `search_tasks` tool returns task UUIDs, assignee UUIDs and project UUIDs only. The agent often invents assignee names in its answers. Which change best follows Anthropic's tool guidance?
options: Resolve ids to human-readable names, keep the ids needed for follow-up calls, and offer a `concise`/`detailed` `response_format`
Return the full raw database row for every task
Tell the agent in the system prompt never to guess names
Hash the UUIDs so they are shorter
questions.explanation: Anthropic reports that resolving opaque UUIDs to meaningful names reduced hallucinations, and recommends a response_format enum so the agent can choose concise output or detailed output with identifiers for later calls. Raw rows waste tokens and shorter hashes are still opaque.
rationales: Correct. Meaningful context plus a format choice is the documented approach.
Raw rows add noise and tokens without making ids meaningful.
The model cannot avoid guessing names it was never given.
Shorter opaque ids are still opaque.

sources.title: Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: Log search
questions.stem: A `search_logs` tool returns every matching line, often tens of thousands of tokens, and the agent loses track of its task. Which redesign is best?
options: Return the results as a compressed base64 blob
Silently cut the output at a fixed size
Add pagination and filters (time range, service, level), and when results are cut, say how many matched and how to narrow or fetch the next page
Move the log search into the system prompt
questions.explanation: Anthropic recommends pagination, range selection, filtering and truncation for token efficiency, with truncation and error messages that give actionable guidance. Silent truncation hides missing data, and encoded blobs are unreadable to the model.
rationales: The model cannot reason over a compressed blob.
Silent truncation leaves the model unaware that data is missing.
Correct. Fewer, targeted results with guidance on getting more.
Results belong in tool results, not the system prompt.

sources.title: Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: MCP server errors
questions.stem: An MCP server reports a failed date validation ("end_date before start_date") as a JSON-RPC error. The host shows a generic failure and the model never gets a chance to fix the dates. What does the MCP spec say the server should do?
options: Keep the JSON-RPC error; all failures are protocol errors
Return a tool result with `isError: true` and a message explaining the problem, so the client can pass it to the model
Silently swap the two dates and return success
Close the connection so the client retries
questions.explanation: The MCP tools spec reserves protocol errors for things like unknown tools and malformed requests. Input validation, API failures and business-logic errors are tool execution errors returned in the result with isError: true, and clients SHOULD pass them to the model so it can self-correct.
rationales: Validation failures are execution errors, not protocol errors.
Correct. The model sees the error and can retry with fixed input.
Guessing the user's intent can do the wrong thing silently.
Dropping the connection gives the model nothing to act on.

questions.scenario: Structured tool results
questions.stem: An MCP tool declares an `outputSchema` for order status. Which two statements about its results match the MCP spec? (Select two.)
options: `structuredContent` must conform to the declared `outputSchema`
For backwards compatibility, the tool should also return the serialized JSON in a text content block
Declaring an `outputSchema` means the tool no longer needs an `inputSchema`
`structuredContent` must always be a string
questions.explanation: When an outputSchema is given, structuredContent must conform to it, and the spec recommends also returning the serialized JSON as text for clients that do not read structured content. The input schema is separate, and structuredContent may be any JSON value.
rationales: Correct. Conformance is required when a schema is declared.
Correct. The text copy keeps older clients working.
Input and output schemas are independent.
structuredContent may be any JSON value.

questions.scenario: Shopping basket tool
questions.stem: A stateless MCP server lets agents build a shopping basket across calls by returning a basket handle. Which handle design follows MCP's guidance?
options: Sequential integers (1, 2, 3) so the model can remember them easily
An opaque handle that, once issued, is accepted as proof of the user's identity
The user's email address, since it is already unique
An opaque, high-entropy handle such as `bsk_a1b2c3`, authorization-checked on every call, with its lifetime stated in the description and an expiry reported as a tool execution error
questions.explanation: MCP's stateful-tools guidance calls for explicit opaque, high-entropy handles, authorization checked on every call, the lifetime documented, and expiry returned as a tool execution error. Guessable ids invite hijacking, and a handle is not authentication: bind it to the verified user server-side.
rationales: Guessable handles let one user reach another's state.
A handle is not authentication; authorization must be checked every time.
Personal data as a handle leaks information and is guessable.
Correct. This matches the documented handle properties.

questions.scenario: Duplicate payment
questions.stem: A `send_payment` call timed out, but the payment had actually gone through. The agent retried and the customer was charged twice. Which design prevents this?
options: Generate an idempotency key once per logical payment in the orchestration code and send the same key on every retry, so the server returns the first result
Tell the agent in its prompt never to retry payments
Generate a fresh idempotency key on every HTTP attempt
Shorten the timeout so the call fails faster
questions.explanation: Idempotency keys let a server recognise a repeated request and return the stored result instead of acting again. The key must identify the logical operation and be reused across retries; a new key per attempt makes every retry a new payment. Prompt rules and shorter timeouts do not make the write safe to repeat.
rationales: Correct. One key per operation, reused on retry.
Prompt rules are not a guarantee, and some retries are legitimate.
A new key per attempt defeats the purpose.
A shorter timeout makes ambiguous outcomes more likely, not less.

questions.scenario: Auto-approval policy
questions.stem: A host auto-approves any MCP tool whose annotations set `readOnlyHint: true`. A newly installed third-party server labels its `delete_repository` tool read-only. What principle does this policy violate?
options: Annotations are only valid on tools with an `outputSchema`
Read-only tools must always set `openWorldHint: false`
Annotations must be treated as untrusted unless they come from a trusted server
Only the host may set `readOnlyHint`
questions.explanation: The MCP tools spec says clients MUST consider tool annotations untrusted unless they come from trusted servers, and the schema notes that annotations are hints that are not guaranteed to describe tool behaviour faithfully. A malicious or buggy server can mislabel destructive tools, so approval policy cannot rest on annotations alone. Hosts should also keep a human able to deny invocations.
rationales: Annotations do not depend on an output schema.
openWorldHint is independent of read-only status.
Correct. Annotations are hints, not guarantees.
Servers set annotations; the issue is trusting them.

questions.scenario: Bulk cleanup tool
questions.stem: You are designing a `delete_old_exports` tool that can remove thousands of files. Which two measures make it safer for an agent to use? (Select two.)
options: A `dry_run` mode that returns exactly which files would be deleted, without deleting anything
A confirmation step in the host before the destructive call runs
Annotating it `destructiveHint: false` so users are not bothered with prompts
Trusting the model to state in its reply that it checked the list
questions.explanation: A dry run lets the agent or a human see the exact change set before anything happens, and the MCP spec says clients SHOULD prompt for confirmation on sensitive operations. Mislabelling annotations removes a safeguard, and a model's statement is not a control.
rationales: Correct. Preview before acting.
Correct. Human confirmation for destructive operations.
Mislabelling the tool hides its risk.
A model's claim is not verification.

questions.scenario: Unannotated tools
questions.stem: An MCP server publishes a `sync_inventory` tool with no annotations at all. Under the MCP annotation defaults, how should a cautious client treat it?
options: As read-only and idempotent, because nothing says otherwise
As a potentially destructive, non-idempotent write that may touch external systems
As unusable until annotations are added
As safe to retry automatically
questions.explanation: The MCP schema documents the ToolAnnotations defaults: readOnlyHint false, destructiveHint true, idempotentHint false and openWorldHint true. A tool with no annotations should therefore be treated as a possibly destructive, non-idempotent, open-world write, which argues for confirmation and no blind retries.
rationales: The defaults assume the opposite.
Correct. That is what the defaults describe.
Annotations are optional; the tool is usable.
idempotentHint defaults to false, so blind retries are unsafe.

questions.scenario: Coding agent sandbox
questions.stem: A coding agent runs shell commands in a sandbox that restricts writes to the project directory but leaves network access open. A prompt-injected README makes it upload the repository's `.env` file to an attacker's server. What does Anthropic's sandboxing guidance say was missing?
options: A larger model that ignores injected instructions
A shorter command timeout
A read-only root filesystem
Network isolation, for example a proxy that only allows approved domains; effective sandboxing needs both filesystem and network isolation
questions.explanation: Anthropic's Claude Code sandboxing post states that effective sandboxing requires both filesystem and network isolation. Without network controls, code can exfiltrate whatever it can read. Claude Code routes traffic through a proxy that restricts domains.
rationales: Model choice is not an isolation boundary.
The upload can complete well within any reasonable timeout.
The file was readable inside the project; more filesystem limits do not stop the upload.
Correct. The missing wall was network isolation.

questions.scenario: Spreadsheet analysis
questions.stem: An agent fetches a 10,000-row sheet through an MCP tool, passes it through the model, then sends it to another tool, consuming a large share of the context. Which approach does Anthropic's code-execution-with-MCP post describe?
options: Present MCP servers as code APIs so the agent writes code that fetches, filters and passes data inside a sandbox, returning only the small result to the model
Ask the model to summarise the sheet before forwarding it
Increase the tool-response token limit
Load every MCP tool definition up front so the model can plan better
questions.explanation: The post describes presenting MCP servers as code APIs on a filesystem; code filters and aggregates data and intermediate data can stay in the sandbox. In its example token use fell from 150,000 to 2,000. Summarising or raising limits still pushes the full sheet through the context.
rationales: Correct. Data stays in the execution environment.
The model still has to read the whole sheet to summarise it.
A higher limit makes the problem bigger.
Loading all definitions up front is part of the token problem.

sources.title: Code execution with MCP — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: Running model-written code
questions.stem: Your agent will execute Python it writes itself. Which three controls belong in the execution environment? (Select three.)
options: A wall-clock timeout on each execution
CPU, memory and disk limits on the sandbox
Network egress restricted to an allowlist
Running on the developer's host with their cloud credentials so tools just work
questions.explanation: Anthropic's code-execution post says agent-written code needs sandboxing, resource limits and monitoring; its sandboxing post adds that effective sandboxing needs network isolation as well as filesystem isolation; and the MCP spec says clients SHOULD set timeouts on tool calls. Running on a host with ambient credentials gives injected or buggy code everything it needs to do damage.
rationales: Correct. Stops runaway loops and hung calls.
Correct. Contains resource exhaustion.
Correct. Limits exfiltration and lateral movement.
Ambient credentials on a host turn any bad code into a real incident.

sources.title: Code execution with MCP — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: Computer use agent
questions.stem: A team adds Claude computer use to automate a back-office web app. Where does the responsibility for isolating the actions lie?
options: With Anthropic, because computer use is a server tool that runs in Anthropic's cloud
With the web app, which must detect automated clicks
With the team, because computer use is a client tool their own code executes, so they must run it in an isolated, minimally privileged environment
Nowhere, because screenshots cannot cause side effects
questions.explanation: The Claude tool-use overview lists computer use (and the browser toolset) among Anthropic-schema client tools: your application executes the actions. That makes isolation, privileges and confirmations the team's job. Clicks and keystrokes can certainly cause side effects.
rationales: Computer use is a client tool, not a server tool.
The app being automated is not the safety boundary.
Correct. Your code runs it, so you isolate it.
Mouse and keyboard actions can purchase, delete or send.

questions.scenario: A team is adding a 'weekly status report' to their MCP server. Users always want it attached when they start a planning conversation, and they pick it from a menu. Today it is a tool, and the model often forgets to call it.
questions.stem: Which change best fits the MCP control model?
options: Expose it as a prompt the user selects (or a resource the host attaches), since the user, not the model, decides when it is needed.
Make it a sampling request so the server can ask the model to summarise the week.
Expose it as an elicitation so the server asks the user whether to include it.
Keep it as a tool and add 'ALWAYS call this first' to its description.
questions.explanation: MCP assigns control by primitive: prompts are user-controlled, resources application-controlled and tools model-controlled. Content the user chooses from a menu fits a prompt, and context the app attaches fits a resource. Forcing the model to remember a tool call fights that model.
rationales: Correct. The user chooses it, so it belongs to a user- or application-controlled primitive.
Sampling is deprecated in 2026-07-28 and does not solve who decides to include the report.
Elicitation gathers user input for a request in progress; it is not a way to publish content.
Description shouting is an anti-pattern and still leaves the decision with the model.

questions.scenario: A client built for MCP 2026-07-28 sends `tools/call` to a server and gets a JSON-RPC error `-32022` with `data: { supported: ["2025-11-25"], requested: "2026-07-28" }`.
questions.stem: What is the correct client behaviour?
options: Resend the same request with a new id, since the error is transient.
Send an `initialize` request with the 2026-07-28 version to open a session first.
Treat the server as broken and surface an error to the user.
Retry with a version from the `supported` list that the client also implements, or report incompatibility if there is none.
questions.explanation: In 2026-07-28 there is no handshake; the server rejects an unsupported version with -32022 and lists what it supports, and the client retries with a mutually supported version. Here that is the older era, so the client must actually speak 2025-11-25 to proceed.
rationales: Repeating the same version will fail the same way.
The 2026-07-28 revision has no `initialize` handshake for its own version.
The error is a normal negotiation step, not a fault.
Correct. The `supported` list is there so the client can pick a version and retry.

questions.scenario: A platform team is reviewing a server's request handling for the 2026-07-28 revision.
questions.stem: Which two statements about per-request metadata are correct? (Select two.)
options: `io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion` and `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities` are required in `_meta` on every request.
Capabilities are negotiated once per connection and then omitted for speed.
`clientInfo` is self-reported and should not drive security decisions.
A request missing a required `_meta` field should be served using the server's newest version.
questions.explanation: The base protocol makes protocol version and client capabilities required on every request, and a missing required field is rejected with -32602. Client and server info are self-reported, so they must not be used for security decisions.
rationales: Correct. Both fields are required per request.
There is no per-connection negotiation; requests are self-contained.
Correct. Self-reported identity is not a security signal.
A missing required field is an error (-32602, HTTP 400), not a cue to guess.

questions.scenario: A server returns a `tools/call` result with no `resultType` field. The client implements 2026-07-28.
questions.stem: How should the client interpret the result?
options: As a protocol error, because `resultType` is mandatory.
As `complete`, because a missing `resultType` from an older server is treated that way.
As a partial result, and wait for a follow-up notification.
As `input_required`, and prompt the user for more information.
questions.explanation: Every 2026-07-28 result carries `resultType`, either complete or input_required. For compatibility with older servers, a missing value is treated as complete.
rationales: The spec defines a fallback rather than an error.
Correct. Missing means complete.
There is no partial-result follow-up mechanism implied by a missing field.
input_required must be signalled explicitly with its input requests.

questions.scenario: A product manager reads that Sampling is deprecated in MCP 2026-07-28 and asks the team to rip out sampling support from their host this sprint.
questions.stem: What is the most accurate response?
options: Explain that Sampling was only renamed to Elicitation and nothing changes.
Explain that deprecation only applies to stdio transports.
Agree: deprecated features are removed immediately and servers will start failing.
Explain that deprecations follow a minimum 12-month window, so plan a migration while it still works.
questions.explanation: The 2026-07-28 changelog sets a minimum 12-month deprecation window. Deprecated is not removed; it is a signal to migrate. Elicitation is a different feature, for asking the user for input.
rationales: Elicitation asks the user; sampling asked the client's model. They are not the same feature.
Deprecation is about the feature, not a transport.
Deprecated features are not removed immediately.
Correct. There is a minimum 12-month window.

questions.scenario: A long-running `tools/call` over Streamable HTTP (2026-07-28) is streaming progress on a request-scoped SSE response. The user clicks Stop.
questions.stem: How should the client cancel the request?
options: Close the response stream for that request.
Send DELETE to the MCP endpoint with the session id.
Send `ping` and wait for the server to time out.
POST a `notifications/cancelled` message with the request id.
questions.explanation: On Streamable HTTP in 2026-07-28, cancellation is closing the response stream; `notifications/cancelled` is the stdio mechanism. Sessions and DELETE were removed, and `ping` was removed too.
rationales: Correct.
There are no sessions and DELETE was removed (modern servers answer 405).
`ping` was removed and would not cancel anything.
That is the stdio mechanism; HTTP cancellation is closing the stream.

questions.scenario: A mobile client loses connectivity halfway through a request-scoped SSE response from a 2026-07-28 server. When the network returns, the developer wants to pick up where the stream left off.
questions.stem: What should the client do?
options: Reconnect with `Last-Event-ID` to resume the stream.
Open a GET stream on the endpoint to receive the remaining events.
Re-issue the request with a new JSON-RPC id, and design side-effecting tools to tolerate retries.
Send the same JSON-RPC id again so the server can deduplicate.
questions.explanation: Resumability via `Last-Event-ID` and the GET stream were removed in 2026-07-28. A broken stream loses the request, and the client must re-issue it with a new id. Because a retried request may repeat work, side-effecting tools should be designed to tolerate retries.
rationales: `Last-Event-ID` resumability was removed.
The standalone GET stream was removed.
Correct.
The retry must use a new JSON-RPC id.

questions.scenario: A developer is migrating a legacy Streamable HTTP server to 2026-07-28. It currently assigns `Mcp-Session-Id` on initialize and keys a per-user shopping cart on it.
questions.stem: What is the right design under the new revision?
options: Store the cart in memory per TCP connection.
Pass an explicit identifier (for example a cart ID) in each request and keep the state in a store; ignore session headers.
Move the cart into the GET stream so it persists across requests.
Keep `Mcp-Session-Id` but rename it to `Mcp-Name`.
questions.explanation: 2026-07-28 removed `Mcp-Session-Id`; a modern server ignores session headers, and a connection is not a session. State that spans requests is addressed by explicit identifiers passed on each request.
rationales: A connection is explicitly not a session; requests may arrive on different connections.
Correct.
The GET stream was removed.
`Mcp-Name` carries the primitive's name for routing; it is not a session.

questions.scenario: An API gateway in front of several MCP servers wants to route and rate-limit `tools/call` by tool name without parsing JSON bodies. The team also wants to route by a `tenant_api_key` parameter.
questions.stem: Which two approaches are consistent with the 2026-07-28 transport? (Select two.)
options: Route on the `Mcp-Method` and `Mcp-Name` headers.
Mark `tenant_api_key` with `x-mcp-header` so it is mirrored into an `Mcp-Param-` header.
Mirror only non-secret primitive parameters, such as a tenant ID, with `x-mcp-header`.
Route on `Mcp-Session-Id`, which identifies the tenant.
questions.explanation: Streamable HTTP sends `Mcp-Method` on every request and `Mcp-Name` on tools/call, resources/read and prompts/get, so gateways can route without parsing bodies. `x-mcp-header` mirrors a primitive parameter into an `Mcp-Param-{Name}` header, which should never be done for secrets because headers are widely logged.
rationales: Correct. These headers exist for routing.
Secrets must not be marked with `x-mcp-header`.
Correct. Non-secret routing keys are the intended use.
Session IDs were removed.

questions.scenario: A developer runs a local Streamable HTTP MCP server for a desktop host. It listens on 0.0.0.0:3000 and accepts any `Origin` header.
questions.stem: What should change first?
options: Switch to the deprecated HTTP+SSE transport, which has built-in origin checks.
Require `Mcp-Session-Id` on every request.
Nothing; local servers are not reachable by browsers.
Bind to 127.0.0.1 and validate `Origin`, returning 403 for invalid origins, to block DNS rebinding.
questions.explanation: The transport spec requires servers to validate `Origin` (403 if invalid) to prevent DNS-rebinding attacks from web pages, and recommends that local servers bind to 127.0.0.1 rather than all interfaces.
rationales: HTTP+SSE is deprecated and is not the fix.
Sessions were removed and would not stop rebinding.
A malicious page can reach local servers through DNS rebinding.
Correct.

questions.scenario: A `tools/call` handler needs the user to pick a shipping address before it can continue. Under the legacy protocol it sent an `elicitation/create` request to the client mid-call.
questions.stem: How does this work in MCP 2026-07-28?
options: The server sends `elicitation/create` on the request-scoped SSE stream.
The server returns a result with `resultType: "input_required"` and a `requestState`; the client collects input and retries the original call with a new id, echoing `requestState` unchanged.
The server opens a GET stream and pushes the elicitation there.
The server returns `isError: true` asking the model to guess an address.
questions.explanation: Server-initiated requests are gone in 2026-07-28; Multi Round-Trip Requests replace them. The server returns input_required with input requests and opaque state, and the client retries with a new JSON-RPC id, echoing the state exactly. The server must not send requests on the response stream.
rationales: Servers must not send requests on the response stream.
Correct. This is the MRTR pattern.
The GET stream was removed.
Guessing user data is wrong; the user should be asked through elicitation.

questions.scenario: A team's `package.json` depends on `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.32.x. A reviewer insists the server already speaks the stateless 2026-07-28 protocol because it uses `StreamableHTTPServerTransport` with `sessionIdGenerator: undefined`.
questions.stem: What is accurate?
options: v1 and v2 are identical; v2 only renames the package.
Correct: that option switches v1 to 2026-07-28.
Not quite: v1 implements the spec up to 2025-11-25; that option is only v1's nearest stateless mode. 2026-07-28 needs the v2 packages `@modelcontextprotocol/server`/`client`.
Correct, as long as `enableJsonResponse` is also true.
questions.explanation: The v1 maintenance line implements MCP up to 2025-11-25, and support for 2026-07-28 is not planned for it. Turning off session IDs is the closest v1 gets to stateless operation, but the wire protocol is still the older era. The v2 packages implement 2026-07-28.
rationales: v2 is a different API and protocol era, not just a rename.
The option does not change the protocol revision.
Correct.
JSON responses do not change the revision either.

sources.title: TypeScript SDK repository — Model Context Protocol
Upgrade to v2 — MCP TypeScript SDK

questions.scenario: A `get_invoice` tool calls a billing API. When the invoice ID does not exist, the handler currently throws `new Error("not found")`.
questions.stem: What is the best way to report this?
